neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said: be my heirs in the teaching. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad uses the same word. The scholars are the heirs of the prophets, it says, and the prophets left no gold or silver coins as inheritance; they left knowledge, and whoever takes it takes a great share.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the knowledge passed down is revelation from God, carried by prophets. The Buddha's teaching is what he found and taught himself, inherited by anyone who practices it.
neighbors.shared: the best inheritance fits in the heart.
neighbors.sources: Sunan Abi Dawud and Jami' at-Tirmidhi, from Abu al-Darda (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 3

neighbors.heading: whiter than snow
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said a stained cloth won't take dye, so wash it first. A psalm Catholics pray often asks for that washing: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." The Church prays this psalm, the Miserere, as a song of sorrow and fresh starts.
neighbors.difference: In the psalm, God does the washing, out of mercy; Catholics receive that cleansing in baptism and confession. In MN 7, a person sees each stain as a stain and lets it go.
neighbors.shared: a stained heart can be clean again.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 50:9 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 51:7 in many Bibles) · Majjhima Nikaya 7

neighbors.heading: washed by the Name
neighbors.text: Today a dirty cloth came out of the dye patchy and dull. Guru Nanak used the same kitchen-sink picture in the Japji. When hands and feet and body are dirty, he says, water washes them; when clothes are soiled, soap cleans them. But when the mind is stained by wrongdoing, it is washed by love of the Name.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the cleansing comes through love of God's Name and the Guru's grace. In the Buddha's simile, the cloth is cleaned by seeing and dropping the stains, and the dye is trust and goodwill.
neighbors.shared: the stain is not the whole cloth.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4 (Japji 20, Guru Nanak, paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 7

neighbors.heading: the heart follows
neighbors.text: Today a path got worn across a lawn, and the Buddha said the mind leans where thoughts keep going. A medieval Jewish book on the commandments, the Sefer HaChinuch, says something close about deeds: a person is shaped by what they do, and the heart and its thoughts are drawn after the actions. Do good often, and the heart follows.
neighbors.difference: The Chinuch starts from deeds: that's why, it says, the Torah gives so many commandments to do. The Buddha starts here from thoughts, sorting them and steering the mind.
neighbors.shared: what we repeat, we slowly become.

neighbors.heading: dyed by thoughts
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said the mind inclines toward whatever it thinks about often. Marcus Aurelius wrote it to himself in his notebook: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts." So, he says, keep dyeing it with good ones.
neighbors.difference: Marcus trains his thoughts to live in line with reason and nature, the Stoic way. The Buddha sorts thoughts by whether they lead to harm, on a path toward freedom from craving.
neighbors.shared: the mind takes the color of what it holds.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.16 (Long 1862) · Majjhima Nikaya 19

neighbors.heading: what remains
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha named two searches: one for things that age like us, one for what doesn't age. The Qur'an draws the same line in one short sentence: "That which ye have wasteth away, and that which Allah hath remaineth." Wealth and children are a joy of this world, another verse says, but good deeds that last are better.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, what lasts is with God, and good deeds are kept by Him. The Buddha's deathless is nibbana, the ending of craving, not a gift from a creator.
neighbors.shared: some things are worth more than a lifetime of searches.

neighbors.heading: the good and the pleasant
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said there is a noble search and an ignoble one. In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches the boy Nachiketa the same fork. The good and the pleasant both come to a person, Death says. The wise one weighs them and chooses the good; the fool chooses the pleasant, for the sake of getting and keeping.
neighbors.difference: Nachiketa's search leads to the Self, the deathless one within. The Buddha sought the deathless too, but taught it without a lasting Self to find.
neighbors.shared: it's worth asking what we're really searching for.

neighbors.heading: proud of tall houses
neighbors.text: Today a god showed off his palace instead of listening, until a monk shook it with his toe. Kabir's verses in the Guru Granth Sahib give a similar shake. Kabir, he says, don't be proud, looking at your tall mansions. Today or tomorrow you'll lie under the ground, and grass will grow over you.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, pride grows from haumai, the ego that hides God; the cure is remembering the Name. Moggallana's shake points to the teaching that nothing, even a heaven, is worth clinging to.
neighbors.shared: even the grandest house is only borrowed.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok of Kabir (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 37

neighbors.heading: bigger barns
neighbors.text: Today Sakka was too busy with his palace to think about the teaching. Jesus told a story about a rich man like that. His harvest was so big he planned bigger barns, and said to himself: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease." But God said to him, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee."
neighbors.difference: Jesus ends with being "rich toward God," an account given to a Maker. Moggallana's lesson is that nothing is worth clinging to, with no one to give an account to.
neighbors.shared: what we hold onto can't hold us up.

neighbors.heading: dare to know
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha gave his monks a method for testing him. Immanuel Kant put the same courage into a short essay on enlightenment. Its motto, he says, is: dare to know. Have the courage to use your own understanding, instead of leaning on someone else's say-so, whether a book, a pastor or a doctor.
neighbors.difference: Kant trusts reason itself to judge. The Buddha asks for watching a teacher's conduct over time, listening and asking, and lets trust grow from what's seen.
neighbors.shared: good teachers welcome good questions.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, What Is Enlightenment? (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 47

neighbors.heading: prove all things
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha invited monks to investigate even him. Saint Paul gave the early Christians a similar instruction: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." And Saint John warns: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God." Faith, for both, isn't swallowing everything that sounds holy.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, testing happens within a faith received from God, with the Church's teaching as guide. The Buddha's method turns on the teacher himself, judged by watching his conduct.
neighbors.shared: honest questions can be part of faith.

neighbors.heading: the guest at the door
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha told Upali to keep feeding the Jain monks who'd always come to his house. Hindus have an old rule for whoever arrives. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher's parting advice says: let the guest be a god to you.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad honors the guest as divine. The Buddha's reason is plainer: Upali's house had long been a well-spring for those monks, and generosity shouldn't stop because his beliefs changed.
neighbors.shared: a changed mind doesn't have to close the door.

neighbors.heading: the ways of peace
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha told a new follower to keep giving to the monks of another teacher. The Talmud asks for a similar generosity across lines. Jews should support the poor of other peoples along with their own, it says, visit their sick and bury their dead, for the sake of the ways of peace.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud grounds this in peace between neighbors living side by side. The Buddha grounds it in Upali's long friendship with those monks, and in giving that doesn't keep score of creeds.
neighbors.shared: kindness doesn't check which line you're in.

neighbors.heading: truth in love
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said he'd speak an unwelcome truth only if it helps, at the right time, like pulling a stick from a baby's throat. Paul wrote about the same balance: "speaking the truth in love," and, "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."
neighbors.difference: Paul's measure is building up the church in Christ. The Buddha's three tests, true, beneficial, well-timed, come from his care for the listener, not from a call to build up a church in Christ.
neighbors.shared: a hard truth can still be a kind one.

neighbors.heading: say good, or be quiet
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha weighed every word: is it true, is it helpful, is it time? A well-known saying of the Prophet Muhammad gives a simple test: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let them say what is good, or stay silent.
neighbors.difference: The hadith ties speech to faith in God and the Day of Judgment. The Buddha's tests come from care for the listener, and he sometimes chose an unwelcome truth when it would help.
neighbors.shared: some words heal, and some silences do too.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 58

neighbors.heading: the interior castle
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said nobody arrives all at once: you turn up, sit near, listen, and go on. Saint Teresa of Avila pictured the soul as a castle with many rooms. You enter by prayer, she wrote, and move inward room by room, not in a leap. Many stay in the outer rooms a long time, and that's where everyone begins.
neighbors.difference: For Teresa, God dwells at the castle's center, and moving inward is his grace as much as our effort. The Buddha's gradual training is walked by effort, toward seeing the truth for oneself.
neighbors.shared: the first step is just showing up.
neighbors.sources: Teresa of Avila, The Interior Castle (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 70

neighbors.heading: five realms
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha laid out a dozen gradual steps. Guru Nanak's Japji also climbs in stages. It names five realms: the realm of duty, where deeds are weighed; the realm of knowledge; the realm of effort; the realm of grace; and the realm of truth, where the Formless One dwells.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the higher realms open by grace, and the last is the dwelling of God. The Buddha's steps run from faith to seeing the truth for oneself, without a creator at the end.
neighbors.shared: every big journey is made of small steps.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji 34–37 (Guru Nanak, paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 70

neighbors.heading: number our days
neighbors.text: Today a king read his first gray hair as a messenger. A psalm asks for that kind of reading: "So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom." The psalm sets a human life, short as grass, beside God, for whom a thousand years are like yesterday.
neighbors.difference: The psalm asks God for a wise heart within the life one already has. Makhadeva read his gray hair as the sign to leave home and go forth.
neighbors.shared: a reminder of time can be a gift.

neighbors.heading: while you can
neighbors.text: Today the barber laid a gray hair in the king's palm. Marcus Aurelius, an emperor too, wrote himself the same reminder: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good."
neighbors.difference: Marcus stayed on the throne and used the reminder to rule and live well. Makhadeva gave up his throne and went forth to practice.
neighbors.shared: the time to be good is today.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.17 (Long 1862) · Majjhima Nikaya 83

neighbors.heading: best in conduct
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said fire from any wood burns the same, whoever lit it. The Qur'an says people were made into nations and tribes so they would know one another, then names what really counts: "the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct."
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, nobility is measured by God, by a person's mindfulness of Him. The Buddha's fire needs no judge: purity is in what each person does.
neighbors.shared: nobody is better because of where they were born.

neighbors.heading: the same in all
neighbors.text: Today a young brahmin argued that birth decides purity, and the Buddha answered with fire. The Bhagavad Gita has a line on seeing alike. The wise, Krishna says, see the same in a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person who eats dogs. One Self looks out through all.
neighbors.difference: Hindu traditions have long debated whether varna comes by birth or by conduct; the Gita's sameness rests on one Self in every being. The Buddha sets the classes aside and needs no Self.
neighbors.shared: every person can light the same fire.

neighbors.heading: those who loved
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha told Subha the way to Brahma: a heart of kindness, compassion, gladness and calm filling every direction. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a hymn that is part of the Sikh morning prayers. In it he says: I speak the truth, all of you, listen. Those who loved, they found the Lord.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, love is the way to the one Creator, by the Guru's grace. In the sutta, Brahma is a high god the brahmins hoped to join; the Buddha uses their word and doesn't teach a creator.
neighbors.shared: a heart with no edges is never wasted.
neighbors.sources: Dasam Granth, Tav-Prasad Savaiye (Guru Gobind Singh, paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 99

neighbors.heading: God is love
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said the way to companionship with Brahma is a heart filled with love in every direction. The First Letter of John puts it in one line: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, God is love itself, the Creator who loved first. The Brahma of the sutta is a god the brahmins sought, and the four immeasurables are states the practitioner develops.
neighbors.shared: love grows when we live in it.

neighbors.heading: don't call yourself a philosopher
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha drew a true person who doesn't boast of family, learning or long practice. Epictetus gave his students the same advice. Never call yourself a philosopher, he says, and don't talk a lot about principles among people who haven't studied them. Just do what follows from them. Sheep don't show the shepherd how much they ate; they make wool.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus wants philosophy shown in a life lived by reason. The Buddha's true person sees that boasting doesn't end greed, hatred and delusion; only practice does.
neighbors.shared: let the practice speak for itself.

neighbors.heading: puffed up
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha described the untrue person: learned, accomplished, and keen to say so. Saint Paul put it in a few words for the church at Corinth: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." And charity, he says later, "is not puffed up." Learning is good; showing it off misses the point.
neighbors.difference: For Paul, charity is love of God and neighbor, a gift of grace. The Buddha's true person simply practices, seeing that pride in any achievement doesn't end greed, hatred and delusion.
neighbors.shared: love builds up; bragging doesn't.

neighbors.heading: the chariot
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha trained the mind like a wild elephant, tied to a post and taught gently. The Katha Upanishad uses a chariot. The body is the chariot, it says, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins, and the senses the horses. Without understanding, the horses run wild; with it, they're like good horses for a skilled driver.
neighbors.difference: In the Katha, the rider in the chariot is the Self, and the road leads to the highest place of Vishnu. In the Buddha's picture, the elephant is trained step by step, with no rider at the center.
neighbors.shared: an untrained mind can learn, slowly.

neighbors.heading: who is mighty
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said a wild mind can be tamed, one gentle step at a time. The book of Proverbs says: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; And he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." The Mishnah asks: who is mighty? Whoever masters their own inclination.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish thought, mastering the inclination is serving God, and the rabbis even say the inclination has its uses. The Buddha's tamed mind is trained toward stillness and freedom.
neighbors.shared: real strength is quiet.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 16:32 (JPS 1917) · Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 4:1 (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 125

neighbors.heading: no thought for the morrow
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said don't chase the past or lean on the future; see what's here. Jesus says something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
neighbors.difference: Jesus says this because the Father feeds the birds and knows what you need. The Buddha's verse rests on clear seeing of the present, and a reminder that death may come tomorrow.
neighbors.shared: today is enough to carry.

neighbors.heading: a traveler on the road
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha's verse said: do today what needs doing; who knows, death may come tomorrow. A companion of the Prophet, Ibn Umar, said something close: when evening comes, don't wait for morning; when morning comes, don't wait for evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
neighbors.difference: Ibn Umar's words come with the Prophet's advice to live in this world like a traveler, preparing for the hereafter before God. The Buddha points to seeing the present clearly and steadily.
neighbors.shared: this day is the one in your hands.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Umar (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 131

neighbors.heading: perfect joy
neighbors.text: Today Punna said: if they insult me, at least they didn't hit me. Saint Francis told Brother Leo a story like that. Imagine arriving at our own friary, he said, cold, soaked and hungry, and the porter calls us impostors and shuts us out in the snow. If we bear it patiently and kindly, that is perfect joy.
neighbors.difference: Francis finds joy in bearing suffering for love of Christ, who suffered first. Punna's calm comes from not clinging to anything seen, heard or felt, not from sharing in another's suffering.
neighbors.shared: patience can turn a hard welcome into peace.
neighbors.sources: The Little Flowers of St. Francis, on perfect joy (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 145

neighbors.heading: don't strike back
neighbors.text: Today Punna answered every insult and blow without hate. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps verses of the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid with the same spirit. Farid, if someone strikes you with their fists, don't strike them back. Go home, and kiss their feet. Elsewhere he says: answer evil with goodness, and don't let anger fill your mind.
neighbors.difference: Farid's humility is rooted in love of God, and Sikhs read it as the Guru's word. Punna's calm comes from letting go of delight in what he sees and hears.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to hit back.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Angs 1378 and 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 145

neighbors.heading: the grass withereth
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked Rahula, sense by sense: is it permanent? and Rahula looked and said no. Isaiah looked at the same truth: all flesh is grass. "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth; But the word of our God shall stand for ever."
neighbors.difference: Isaiah sets passing things beside something that stands forever: God's word. The Buddha asks whether anything passing is fit to be called mine, and lets go without naming an eternal anchor.
neighbors.shared: seeing things change can make us gentler.

neighbors.heading: a river of passing things
neighbors.text: Today Rahula saw everything at the eye, ear and mind changing. Marcus Aurelius wrote that time is like a river of passing events, with a strong current: no sooner is a thing seen than it's swept away, and another takes its place, and that will be swept away too. Long before him, Heraclitus is remembered for saying you can't step into the same river twice.
neighbors.difference: For the Stoics, change runs inside a rational order, and accepting it means living by nature. The Buddha uses change to see that nothing in it is self, and lets go.
neighbors.shared: everything flows, and we can flow with it.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.43 (paraphrase) · Heraclitus, as reported in Plato, Cratylus 402a (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 147

neighbors.heading: speak good
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha's list of small things put speech near the top: true, gentle, never carrying tales to split people apart. Muslims hold speech close to faith too. The Qur'an, recalling a covenant, says "speak kindly to mankind," and the Prophet taught that whoever believes in God and the Last Day should speak good or stay silent.
neighbors.difference: In the sutta, kind speech is part of a training the Buddha himself lived, on the way to freedom. For Muslims, every word is also weighed before God, and guarding the tongue is part of believing in the Day it's answered for.
neighbors.shared: a kind word is never a small thing.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:83 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, "speak good or keep silent" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: true, kind, helpful
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha's small things included speech that's true, pleasant to the ear, and goes to the heart. Hindus know that shape from the Gita. Krishna calls it the austerity of speech: words that cause no distress, true, pleasant and beneficial, along with regular study of sacred texts. Speaking well, there, is a discipline, an austerity of the tongue.
neighbors.difference: Krishna names good speech as tapas, a self-offering practiced within one's dharma. The Buddha lists it as plain conduct, the small things even an ordinary person could praise, and part of the ground of a path to awakening.
neighbors.shared: your words can be a practice, not just noise.

neighbors.heading: ask about the light
neighbors.text: Today a slave shaved his head, went forth, and a king would rise to greet him. Sikhs carry the same reversal. Guru Nanak taught: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste, for there is no caste in the world beyond. In the langar, king and laborer sit on the same floor and eat the same food.
neighbors.difference: In the sutta, the man is honored because he chose a renunciant's life. For Sikhs, the light is God's own, already in every person, and the honored life is a householder's: working, sharing and remembering God.
neighbors.shared: no one's worth is set by where they started.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Raag Asa, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 349 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: neither bond nor free
neighbors.text: Today a slave went forth, and the king who once owned his days would rise to greet him. Christians hear Paul: "there is neither bond nor free... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Paul even sent a slave, Onesimus, back to his master with a letter asking that he be received "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved."
neighbors.difference: The king honors the man for the life he chose, a renunciant's life. For Christians, that equal standing comes through baptism into Christ, a gift of grace.
neighbors.shared: a changed life deserves a changed welcome.

neighbors.heading: the two can't be split
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha and Sonadanda agreed: virtue and wisdom wash each other, like two hands. Aristotle, in his Ethics, landed in the same place by another road. You can't be good, in the full sense, without practical wisdom, he argued, and you can't be practically wise without good character. Knowing what's right and being someone who does it grow together.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle aims at a flourishing life among fellow citizens, here and now. In the sutta, virtue and wisdom answer a question about who is truly a brahmin, and point further, toward the end of suffering.
neighbors.shared: a good heart and a clear head need each other.

neighbors.heading: wisdom teaches the virtues
neighbors.text: Today virtue and wisdom washed each other, like two hands, and neither could be dropped. Catholics read something close in the Book of Wisdom: "for she teacheth temperance, and prudence, and justice, and fortitude." The Church calls prudence the charioteer of the virtues, the practical wisdom that steers the others, while the virtues give that wisdom a life to steer.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, wisdom is finally a gift of God, and all the virtues are crowned by charity, the love of God and neighbor. The Buddha's pair is trained by the practitioner, aimed at seeing clearly and getting free.
neighbors.shared: being good and seeing clearly are one walk, not two.
neighbors.sources: Wisdom 8:7 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1806 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: four doors of the heart
neighbors.text: Today a monk sounded kindness, compassion, gladness and calm in every direction, like a strong trumpeter. Hindus know four attitudes much like these. Patanjali's Yoga Sutra teaches friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward those who suffer, gladness toward the good, and equanimity toward those who do wrong. Held this way, the sutra says, the mind grows clear and calm.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali matches each attitude to a kind of person, to settle the mind for yoga's deeper stillness. The Buddha has them radiate without limit, everywhere at once, offered to young brahmins seeking union with Brahma.
neighbors.shared: a calm mind starts with how you meet other people.

neighbors.heading: be like him
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked two young brahmins: is the Brahma you seek full of hate, or free of it? Then become like that. The rabbis taught the same move. Be like Him, said Abba Shaul: as He is gracious and compassionate, so be gracious and compassionate. Another teacher said walking after God means clothing the naked and visiting the sick, as God did.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, these are the ways of the one God, who commands them in the Torah. The Buddha meets his listeners' hope of union with Brahma and answers with a practice: a mind made boundless through meditation.
neighbors.shared: you grow toward what you most admire.

neighbors.heading: where moth and rust
neighbors.text: Today a king's golden palaces and elephants were all gone, every one. Christians hear Jesus: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt... But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." And then: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
neighbors.difference: The sutta shows every made thing passing away, and points to a freedom beyond them. Christians hope for treasure that lasts: life with God, which doesn't pass away.
neighbors.shared: hold what you own lightly, and love what lasts.

neighbors.heading: the deeds that endure
neighbors.text: Today every one of a king's golden palaces was gone, with his jeweled palms and his elephants. Muslims hear the Qur'an: "Wealth and children are an ornament of life of the world. But the good deeds which endure are better in thy Lord's sight for reward." And elsewhere: everyone on the earth passes away, and the Face of the Lord remains.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, good deeds endure because God, who remains, keeps them and rewards them on the Day of Judgment. The sutta names no creator; it shows all made things passing and points toward the unconditioned.
neighbors.shared: what you give away outlasts what you keep.

neighbors.heading: the rot of envy
neighbors.text: Today Sakka asked why beings who want peace live in hate, and the Buddha named envy and stinginess. Catholics count envy among the seven capital sins, roots that feed other wrongs. Proverbs puts it bodily: "Soundness of heart is the life of the flesh: but envy is the rottenness of the bones." Its remedy, the Church teaches, is goodwill: rejoicing in another's good.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, envy is a sin against love, healed by grace and humility before God. The Buddha traces it through a chain of causes in the mind, back to how we perceive and think.
neighbors.shared: peace starts when someone else's good stops feeling like your loss.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 14:30 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1866, 2540 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no one a stranger
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said envy and stinginess keep us at war, though everyone wants peace. Guru Arjan sang of what happens when envy goes: I've forgotten my jealousy of others since I found the company of the holy. No one is my enemy, no one a stranger; I get along with everyone.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan credits the change to the sangat and to God's grace, seeing God's light in all. The Buddha answers Sakka by naming causes, step by step, so the root can be found and pulled.
neighbors.shared: envy fades in good company.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Raag Kanara, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1299 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one from among thy brethren
neighbors.text: Today the first people picked a ruler by agreement, one of themselves, and paid him in rice. The Torah's king is one of the people too: "one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee." He must write out a copy of the law and read it all his life, "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren."
neighbors.difference: In the Torah, God chooses the king, and the king stays under God's law. In the sutta, the people choose by agreement, and the story gently pokes at anyone who claims rank by birth.
neighbors.shared: whoever leads is still one of us.

neighbors.heading: the consent of the governed
neighbors.text: Today the first people chose one of their own to keep order, by agreement, not by birth or by heaven. Philosophers like John Locke later argued for something close, a government resting on consent, and the Declaration of Independence put it plainly: governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed." Power, on this view, is lent, not owned.
neighbors.difference: The Declaration rests on rights it says a Creator endowed, and founds a nation's law on them. The sutta tells its story half in fun, to question claims of caste, not to found a state.
neighbors.shared: power works best when it remembers who gave it.
neighbors.sources: Declaration of Independence (1776) · John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as they cared for me
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said a child honors parents thinking: they supported me, so I'll support them. Muslims hear the Qur'an: kindness to parents, and when they grow old, "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them." Then words to pray: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little."
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, kindness to parents comes right after worshipping God alone, as God's command. The sutta frames it as a two-way bond: five duties a child owes, and five a parent owes back.
neighbors.shared: the hands that held you deserve holding back.

neighbors.heading: mother as a god
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha put parents in the east, where the day begins, and named what children and parents owe each other. Hindus hear a teacher's parting words in the Taittiriya Upanishad: matru devo bhava, pitru devo bhava. Let your mother be like a god to you; let your father be like a god to you. Then the teacher, and the guest.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad asks a graduating student to honor parents as divine, as part of living dharma. The sutta keeps the bond human and mutual, with duties flowing from parent to child as well as child to parent.
neighbors.shared: honoring parents starts with remembering what they gave.

neighbors.heading: the mind as farmer
neighbors.text: Today a farmer with five hundred plows told the Buddha to plow, and heard: faith is my seed, wisdom my plow, effort my ox. Guru Nanak sang a farm like that: make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farming, effort the water, your body the field. Let God's Name be the seed, and contentment smooth the soil.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the seed is Naam, God's Name, and the harvest comes by grace. The Buddha's seed is faith in a path, and the harvest is freedom, reached by effort that pulls on without turning back.
neighbors.shared: a life can be farmed, slowly, one season at a time.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Raag Sorath, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 595 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the seed is the word
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha told a farmer he plows too: faith is the seed, discipline the rain. Christians know a sower. Jesus told of seed falling on the path, on rock, among thorns, and on good ground, and explained: "The seed is the word of God." The good ground, he said, is an honest and good heart that keeps the word and bears fruit with patience.
neighbors.difference: In the parable, the seed is God's word and the soil is the listener's heart. In the sutta, faith is the seed the farmer sows himself, tended by his own effort toward freedom.
neighbors.shared: what grows in you depends on what you tend.

neighbors.heading: kindness, measured
neighbors.text: Today we read the loving-kindness discourse whole: may all beings be happy and at ease. Psychologists have tested a practice like it. In a 2008 study, Barbara Fredrickson's team taught working adults loving-kindness meditation, and over the following weeks they reported more daily positive emotions, along with gains like closer relationships and a greater sense of purpose.
neighbors.difference: The study measured what kindness does for the one practicing it. The sutta starts with how to live, upright and gentle, and wishes well to all beings, seen and unseen, for their own sake, on a path to awakening.
neighbors.shared: wishing others well changes the one who wishes.
neighbors.sources: Fredrickson, Cohn, Coffey, Pek and Finkel, "Open Hearts Build Lives," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2008) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: sun on the good and bad
neighbors.text: Today the kindness discourse wished well to all beings, weak or strong, near or far, without exception. Catholics hear Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you," that you may be children of a Father "who maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, this love imitates God the Father and is made possible by grace. The sutta's kindness is a quality of mind trained in meditation, like a mother guarding her only child, offered without reference to a creator.
neighbors.shared: kindness doesn't check who deserves it first.

neighbors.heading: knowing what was done
neighbors.text: Today the Pali word for gratitude, kataññuta, meant knowing what was done for you. Hindus use its Sanskrit twin, kritajna, the grateful one, and its opposite, kritaghna, one who destroys what was done. The Mahabharata tells of an ungrateful man who killed the bird that had fed and sheltered him, and says many wrongs can be atoned for, but not ingratitude.
neighbors.difference: In the epic, ingratitude breaks dharma, the order that holds families and worlds together. The Buddha lists gratitude among the highest blessings, a quality of the heart to notice and train.
neighbors.shared: noticing what someone did for you is where thanks begins.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the story of Gautama and the crane (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: recognizing the good
neighbors.text: Today gratitude was knowing what was done for you. Jews have a phrase with the same shape: hakarat ha-tov, recognizing the good. Rashi finds it even in the plagues. Moses didn't strike the Nile himself, he says, because that water once sheltered him as a baby. So Aaron struck it instead. Gratitude, even toward a river.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, gratitude reaches up to God too, thanked in blessings through the day, starting on waking. The Buddha names it a blessing of the heart, beside humility, contentment and being easy to correct.
neighbors.shared: even a river can be owed a thank-you.

neighbors.heading: content in whatsoever state
neighbors.text: Today the last blessing was a mind the world's ups and downs can touch but not shake: gain and loss, praise and blame. Christians hear Paul, writing in chains: "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound."
neighbors.difference: Paul's steadiness rests on someone: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." The sutta's steadiness comes from seeing the eight conditions as passing, so none of them can take hold.
neighbors.shared: your center can hold on a good day and a bad one.

neighbors.heading: grieve not, exult not
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha named eight worldly conditions, gain and loss, praise and blame among them, and praised a mind they can't shake. The Qur'an speaks to the same two-sided pull. It tells believers that what befalls them is already known to God, "That ye grieve not for the sake of that which hath escaped you, nor yet exult because of that which hath been given."
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, steadiness comes from trusting that every event is written and known by God. The Buddha's way names no writer; it trains the mind to see each condition arise and pass.
neighbors.shared: neither the win nor the loss gets to own you.

neighbors.heading: not as those without hope
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said life is short and uncertain, and taught how to draw out the dart of grief. Catholics don't forbid grief; Jesus wept at a friend's tomb. But Paul writes about those who have died, "that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope." And every November 2, All Souls' Day, the Church prays for the dead.
neighbors.difference: Catholic hope rests on Christ's resurrection; the dead are prayed for and hoped to be met again in God. The sutta draws out the dart by seeing death as part of every born life, and setting lamentation down.
neighbors.shared: grief can be held without being the whole of you.

neighbors.heading: let no one weep for me
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said all clay pots break, and taught how to draw out the dart of lamentation. Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's last instructions, recorded by Baba Sundar in the Sadd: let no one weep for me after I'm gone. Instead, he asked that the praise of God be sung. At Sikh funerals, hymns are sung and Kirtan Sohila is recited.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, death is the soul returning to God, accepted within God's will, the hukam. The Buddha sets grief beside the plain truth that all born things die, and points to a peace beyond birth and death.
neighbors.shared: love for the dead can sound like singing, not only crying.
neighbors.sources: Baba Sundar, Sadd (on Guru Amar Das), Raag Ramkali, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 923 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what is hateful to you
neighbors.text: Today a king and queen admitted no one is dearer to them than themselves, and the Buddha drew the lesson: so harm no other. Jews tell of Hillel, asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot. What is hateful to you, he said, don't do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it.
neighbors.difference: Hillel sums up a Torah Jews receive from God, who says "love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." The Buddha reasons from what every being already feels: you love yourself, and so does everyone else.
neighbors.shared: everyone you meet holds themselves as dear as you do.

neighbors.heading: one word for a lifetime
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said: search every direction, and you find no one dearer than yourself, and so it is for everyone else. Asked for one word to live by all his life, Confucius answered: reciprocity. "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Here it rests on an honest look inward.
neighbors.difference: Confucius offers reciprocity as the art of living well with others, in a family and a state. The Buddha draws it from a king's and queen's honest self-love, as part of a path that does no harm.
neighbors.shared: your own heart is a good guide to someone else's.

neighbors.heading: an elephant in the dark
neighbors.text: Today blind men each touched one part of an elephant, and quarreled. The Muslim poet Rumi tells it in the dark: people feel an elephant in an unlit house. One finds the trunk and says a water pipe, one an ear and says a fan, one a leg and says a pillar. If each had held a candle, he says, their words would have agreed.
neighbors.difference: For Rumi, the candle is a light beyond the senses, the eye of a heart turned toward God. The Buddha tells the story to quarreling monks about views held too tightly, and lets those questions be set down.
neighbors.shared: the part you hold is real, and it isn't the whole.

neighbors.heading: each saw a part
neighbors.text: Today blind men grabbed a trunk, a tusk, a tail, and each swore that was the elephant. Ramakrishna, the Bengali saint, told the same story to people arguing about God. Each had touched one part and was right about that part, he said, and wrong to deny the rest. Each devotee, he taught, sees God in the way they've come close.
neighbors.difference: Ramakrishna's elephant is God, too great for any one view, and he uses it to welcome many paths. In the Udana, the elephant is a lesson about clinging to views, and isn't a picture of God at all.
neighbors.shared: it's worth asking what part the other person is holding.
neighbors.sources: Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna, as recorded by his disciples (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: earn and share
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said that if beings knew the fruit of giving, they wouldn't eat even their last bite without sharing. Sikhs live that at the langar, where anyone can sit and eat. Guru Nanak named the way: one who eats what his own work earns, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, sharing, vand chhakna, goes with honest work and remembering God's Name, often named the three pillars of Sikh life. The Buddha's teaching on giving loosens the stain of stinginess and points to the fruit giving brings.
neighbors.shared: a meal is better when someone else gets a share.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Salok, Raag Sarang, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1245 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all she had
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said that even with one bite left, someone who knew the fruit of giving would share it. Christians remember a poor widow at the temple. Rich people gave large sums; she put in two small coins. Jesus said she gave more than all of them: "she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living."
neighbors.difference: Jesus praises a gift given to God at the temple, out of trust in God. The Buddha praises giving that frees the mind from stinginess and bears its own fruit, without tying it to a creator.
neighbors.shared: the smallest gift can be the biggest one.

neighbors.heading: support isn't enough
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha called parents first teachers, because they bring us up, feed us, and show us the world. Confucius pressed the point further. Supporting your parents, he said, isn't the whole of it; even dogs and horses get fed. Without reverence, what would be the difference? Honor, for him, lives in the attitude as much as the help.
neighbors.difference: Confucius places respect for parents at the root of a well-ordered family and state. The Buddha says a home that honors parents lives with Brahma and with its first teachers, and ties it to gratitude for all they did.
neighbors.shared: the way you treat your parents is a lesson too.

neighbors.heading: the first educators
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said a family that honors mother and father lives with its first teachers. Catholics keep the commandment: "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thou mayst be longlived upon the land." And the Church calls parents the first educators of their children, and the home the first school of Christian life, where forgiveness is learned.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, honoring parents is a commandment from God, and the family is called a domestic church. The Buddha gives a reason anyone can see: parents did so much, bringing us up and feeding us.
neighbors.shared: the first classroom is a kitchen table.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 20:12 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1656-1657, 2223 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: What does being a woman matter

neighbors.heading: Gargi stands up
neighbors.text: Today Mara told the nun Soma a woman's wisdom only reaches two fingers, and she answered: what does being a woman matter, when the mind is steady? Hindus remember Gargi. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, at a king's gathering of sages, she rises and questions the great Yajnavalkya, twice, pressing deeper each time about what everything is woven upon.
neighbors.difference: Gargi asks about Brahman, the ground of all, in a debate before a king. Soma speaks from her own awakening and doesn't argue her case; she recognizes Mara, and he vanishes.
neighbors.shared: a clear mind belongs to whoever trains it.

neighbors.heading: she judged Israel
neighbors.text: Today Mara mocked the nun Soma's two-finger wisdom, and she answered that being a woman doesn't matter to a steady mind. The Hebrew Bible remembers a woman people came to for judgment: "Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, she judged Israel at that time." She sat under a palm tree, the text says, and the children of Israel came up to her.
neighbors.difference: Deborah speaks as a prophet, carrying God's word to her people in a time of war. Soma's authority is her own seeing; her verse says what matters is the mind that knows, not any role.
neighbors.shared: a wise voice is worth hearing, whoever it belongs to.

neighbors.heading: iron sharpeneth iron
neighbors.text: Today Ananda said good friendship was half the holy life, and the Buddha said: no, the whole of it. Christians have Proverbs: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." And Jesus promised something to even the smallest gathering: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the friend at the center is Christ himself, present when believers gather. In the sutta, the good friend is a fellow traveler, and the Buddha calls himself that friend, who points out the path.
neighbors.shared: no one walks the path well alone.

neighbors.heading: the musk carrier
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha told Ananda good friendship isn't half the spiritual life; it's the whole. Muslims remember a picture the Prophet gave. A good companion is like someone carrying musk: he may give you some, you may buy some, or at least you'll enjoy the scent. A bad companion is like a blacksmith's bellows, which may burn your clothes or leave you smelling of smoke.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, good company helps a believer stay close to God and to what God loves. In the sutta, the good friend leads to the noble eightfold path, and the Buddha himself is that friend.
neighbors.shared: you become a little like the people you sit with.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the musk carrier and the bellows (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: an image restored
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said the mind is luminous, stained by visitors that arrive from outside. Catholics speak of something bright underneath too: "And God created man to his own image." The Church teaches that sin disfigures that image but can't erase it, and that grace restores it to its original beauty.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the image is God's, the stain runs deep since the first sin, and healing comes by Christ's grace. The sutta calls the stains visitors, cleaned through one's own training, and doesn't call the mind divine.
neighbors.shared: underneath the mess, something in you is still bright.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 1:27 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 705, 1701 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: washed by the Name
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said the mind shines, stained by defilements that come from outside. Guru Nanak's Japji gives a picture of washing: muddy hands and feet, water cleans them; soiled clothes, soap washes them; a mind stained by wrongdoing is washed by love of the Name. And Guru Amar Das says: O my mind, you are a form of the light.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the light within is God's own light, and the washing comes by God's Name and grace. The sutta doesn't call the luminous mind divine; it's cleared by understanding and training.
neighbors.shared: the dirt is real, and so is the shine under it.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 20, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 4 (paraphrase) · Guru Amar Das, Raag Asa, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 441 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: number our days
neighbors.text: Today the five remembrances: I will age, I will sicken, I will die, I'll be parted from all I love, and my deeds are my own. Jews pray a psalm called a prayer of Moses with the same honesty: "So teach us to number our days, that we may get us a heart of wisdom." Counting the days, there, isn't gloom. It's the road to wisdom.
neighbors.difference: The psalm asks God to teach this, and ends hoping God will establish the work of our hands. The remembrances are said without a prayer, ending on the plain fact that we are heirs of our deeds.
neighbors.shared: remembering you'll die can make today matter more.

neighbors.heading: this very moment
neighbors.text: Today the five remembrances: aging, sickness, death, parting from what we love, and owning our deeds. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius kept a remembrance like that in his private notebook: "Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly." Not fear, for him. A way to live awake.
neighbors.difference: Marcus treats death as nature's way, nothing evil, and aims at virtue in the time he has. The fifth remembrance adds what the Stoic doesn't: we are heirs of our deeds, carried forward beyond this life.
neighbors.shared: your days are numbered, so you can make each one count.

neighbors.heading: repel it with what is better
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha gave five ways to let go of a grudge, starting with wishing the person well on purpose. The Qur'an teaches a similar turn: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." It praises, too, those who control their anger and forgive.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, forgiving is also trust in God, who sees and judges what was done. The Buddha's fifth way says the other person owns their deeds and their results, so you can set the grudge down.
neighbors.shared: a grudge is heavy, and you're allowed to put it down.

neighbors.heading: think the opposite
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha gave five ways to remove a grudge: kindness, compassion, calm, not attending, remembering that deeds have owners. Patanjali's Yoga Sutra offers a method close to the first: when harmful thoughts arise, cultivate their opposite. And Krishna, in the Gita, describes the one dear to him as hating no being, friendly and compassionate to all.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali works on the mind for the stillness of yoga, and Krishna speaks of devotion to God. The Buddha offers five separate ways, from kindness to remembering that each person owns their deeds.
neighbors.shared: you can choose which thought to feed.

items.lessonTitle: A friend gives the hard thing

neighbors.heading: friends who walk with me
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha named a friend who gives what's hard to give, bears what's hard to bear, and doesn't leave you in misfortune. Guru Nanak sang of friends like that: my true friends are the ones who walk with me, and who stand beside me where my account is asked for. Tradition says he sang it to a man named Sajjan, whose name meant friend.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the truest friend is God, and good company helps a soul when its deeds are weighed. The Buddha's seven marks describe a human friend, worth keeping close on the path.
neighbors.shared: a real friend shows up when it costs something.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Raag Suhi, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 729 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: greater love
neighbors.text: Today a friend gives what's hard to give, does what's hard to do, and bears what's hard to bear. Christians hear Jesus, on the night before he died: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." And he told his disciples: "I have called you friends."
neighbors.difference: Christians believe Jesus did what he said, giving his life on the cross for the world. The Buddha's seven marks describe a good friend among ordinary people, someone to seek out, and to become.
neighbors.shared: love shows itself in what it carries for someone else.

neighbors.heading: bonds that continue
neighbors.text: Today Japanese families welcomed their ancestors home for Obon, and Moggallana found a way to feed his mother. Grief researchers have a name for something like this: continuing bonds. Their work suggests that keeping a connection with someone who has died, through memory, ritual or talking to them, can be part of healthy grief, not a failure to let go.
neighbors.difference: The researchers make no claim about where the dead are, only about how the living carry them. Obon rests on Buddhist teaching about rebirth, and on merit, made through gifts to monks, truly reaching the dead.
neighbors.shared: the people we've lost can still have a place at the table.
neighbors.sources: Klass, Silverman and Nickman, Continuing Bonds: New Understandings of Grief (1996) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a holy and wholesome thought
neighbors.text: Today Moggallana, helped by the monks, fed his mother among the hungry ghosts, and Japanese families welcome their dead home. Catholics pray for their dead too. Their Bible says: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." Each November 2, All Souls' Day, the Church remembers all the faithful departed.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, prayers and Masses help souls in purgatory on their way to God. In the Ullambana story, offerings to the monastic community make merit that reaches Moggallana's mother among the hungry ghosts.
neighbors.shared: love for the dead can still do something.
neighbors.sources: 2 Maccabees 12:46 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1032 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a fortnight for the ancestors
neighbors.text: Today Chinese communities set out food for hungry ghosts in the seventh month, and the old verses picture the dead waiting outside the walls for what their relatives give. Hindus keep a time like that, Pitru Paksha, the ancestors' fortnight, when families offer rice balls, pinda, and water to their forebears in the shraddha rite, and feed others in their name.
neighbors.difference: In shraddha, the offerings go to the pitrs, the family's ancestors, to sustain them. In the Buddhist verses, the dead are helped by merit: relatives give to the monastic community and dedicate the good to them.
neighbors.shared: remembering the dead can be done with food, and with care.
neighbors.sources: Manusmriti, chapter 3, on the shraddha rite (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a candle and a gift
neighbors.text: Today the old verses pictured the dead waiting outside the walls for what their relatives give. Jews remember their dead on fixed days too. On a yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death, a candle burns through the day and mourners say Kaddish. At Yizkor, said on certain holy days, it's customary to pledge charity in the name of someone who has died.
neighbors.difference: Jewish practice sets out no food for the dead. The Kaddish praises God, and charity given in a loved one's memory is for the elevation of their soul. The Buddhist verses describe the dead as beings who can receive merit.
neighbors.shared: the dead are remembered well by the good we do for them.
neighbors.sources: Jewish mourning customs: yahrzeit, Kaddish and Yizkor (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: depart from evil, and do good
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha's teaching in one verse: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind." Christians pray the Psalms in the same order: "Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it." And Jesus blessed the inner part: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, a pure heart comes through God's grace, and the pure in heart are promised God's presence. The Dhammapada's mind is purified by one's own training, and its verse is called the teaching of all the awakened.
neighbors.shared: stop the harm, do the good, and tend the heart.

neighbors.heading: good deeds annul ill deeds
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha's teaching in one verse: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. The Qur'an joins these too. It swears by the soul and says the one who purifies it succeeds, and the one who buries it in wrong fails. It promises: "Lo! good deeds annul ill deeds." And it asks for a community that enjoins right and forbids wrong.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, purifying the soul is done before God, who forgives and judges. The Dhammapada's verse names no judge; good and harm bear their own fruit, and purity is a mind made clear.
neighbors.shared: every day is a fresh chance to do good.

neighbors.heading: remember you are dust
neighbors.text: Today the prince saw a dead man carried by and wondered how a whole street could keep laughing. Catholics keep that question close on purpose. On Ash Wednesday, ashes go on the forehead with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." And an old book of wisdom says: "In all thy works remember thy last end."
neighbors.difference: For the prince, facing death starts a search for freedom from the whole round of birth and death. For Catholics, remembering death points toward judgment and the hope of rising again with Christ.
neighbors.shared: looking at death honestly can wake you up to how to live.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 3:19 (Douay-Rheims) · Ecclesiasticus 7:40 (Douay-Rheims; Sirach 7:36 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: today or tomorrow
neighbors.text: Today the prince learned that death comes to everyone, high or low, and the color drained out of the gardens. Sikhs sing the same honest truth. In verses of Guru Tegh Bahadur near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says whatever has been made will pass away, today or tomorrow, so sing God's praise and let go of the other tangles.
neighbors.difference: The prince's shock sends him out to end rebirth itself. For Sikhs, the answer to death is remembering God's Name while living a full householder's life, without leaving home.
neighbors.shared: death is certain, so today is worth spending well.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (Guru Tegh Bahadur) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the eye is never full
neighbors.text: Today the prince told a king that pleasures are like fuel on a fire: feed them and they grow. A Jewish wise man noticed the same hunger. Ecclesiastes says: "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing." And the sages asked, who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion.
neighbors.difference: The prince leaves pleasure behind for a homeless life. Jewish teaching tends to bless pleasures rather than flee them: one Talmud passage says a person will answer for every permitted good thing they saw and didn't enjoy.
neighbors.shared: enough is something you notice, not something you buy.
neighbors.sources: Ecclesiastes 1:8 (JPS 1917) · Pirkei Avot 4:1 (paraphrase) · Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin 4:12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the treadmill of wanting
neighbors.text: Today the prince said a fire isn't quenched by fuel. Psychologists found something like it and named it the hedonic treadmill: a raise or a bigger home lifts us for a while, then we get used to it and want the next thing. Long before them, the Roman philosopher Seneca wrote that the poor person isn't the one with little, but the one who craves more.
neighbors.difference: The prince sees craving as part of a burning that only full freedom ends. Psychology mostly asks how to live well alongside it: gratitude, savoring, and spending on time and people rather than things.
neighbors.shared: the next thing rarely fills the space we hoped it would.
neighbors.sources: Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell, "Hedonic Relativism and Planning the Good Society" (paraphrase) · Seneca, Moral Letters 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the whisperer who makes it pretty
neighbors.text: Today Mara came with a bow of flowers, appealing first to duty and pleasure, and only then to fear. The Qur'an knows a tempter too. Iblis tells God: "I verily shall adorn the path of error for them in the earth." And Muslims ask God's protection "from the evil of the sneaking whisperer," who whispers in people's hearts.
neighbors.difference: In the poem, Mara is turned back by the prince's own resolve under the tree. In Islam, Satan is a creature under God, and the shelter is turning to God: the Qur'an says he has no power over God's true servants.
neighbors.shared: temptation often arrives dressed as something sweet and sensible.

neighbors.heading: the god with the flower bow
neighbors.text: Today Mara came as the god of love, with flowers on his bow and his arrows. Hindus know that archer. Kama, the god of desire, carries a bow of sugarcane and arrows tipped with flowers. In the old stories he aims one at Shiva, deep in meditation, and Shiva opens his third eye and burns him to ash.
neighbors.difference: Ashvaghosha joins love and Mara into one enemy of freedom. In Hindu tradition Kama isn't simply an enemy: desire is one of life's four aims, honored in its place, and Kama is later restored, without a body.
neighbors.shared: even a mind in deep stillness gets tested by desire.
neighbors.sources: Kalidasa, Kumarasambhava 3 (paraphrase) · Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the word, set to music
neighbors.text: Today a monk-poet said he mixed his teaching with beauty, like honey around medicine, so listeners would stay. Sikhs sing their scripture. The hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are arranged by raga, musical mode, and sung as kirtan in the gurdwara. Tradition says Guru Nanak traveled with a musician, Bhai Mardana, who played the rabab while the Guru sang.
neighbors.difference: Ashvaghosha says the poetry is only honey: keep the gold and let the rest wash away. For Sikhs the sung words are themselves the Guru's word, gurbani, not a wrapper around it.
neighbors.shared: a song can carry a truth further than a lecture.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, arranged by raga (paraphrase) · the Janamsakhis, on Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: psalms and hymns
neighbors.text: Today a poet said he wrote in verse so people would stay long enough to hear the teaching. Christians have sung their faith from the start. Paul wrote to one church: "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." And a whole book of the Bible, the Psalms, is songs.
neighbors.difference: Ashvaghosha treats beauty as honey that helps the medicine down, and asks readers to keep only what leads to peace. Christians often see beautiful song as itself a way of praising God, not only a carrier.
neighbors.shared: beauty can open a door that an argument can't.

neighbors.heading: a person, not a label
neighbors.text: Today a young woman told Ananda her caste, and he answered that he had asked for water, not for her birth. The philosopher Martin Buber described that kind of moment. We can meet someone as an it, a category to sort, or as a you, a whole person in front of us. Real living, he thought, happens in the second kind of meeting.
neighbors.difference: Ananda's answer rests on the Buddha's teaching that no one is low by birth, only by what they do. Buber's rests on the meeting itself: what happens between two people who truly see each other.
neighbors.shared: the person in front of you is more than the box they're in.

neighbors.heading: give me to drink
neighbors.text: Today Ananda asked a young woman at a well for water, and she stepped back, naming the line between them. Catholics read a scene much like it. Jesus, tired at a well, asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, and she answers: "How dost thou, being a Jew, ask of me to drink, who am a Samaritan woman?" He keeps talking with her anyway.
neighbors.difference: Ananda's answer sets caste aside so a cup of water can pass. In John's Gospel, Jesus goes on to offer the woman "living water," and the scene becomes about who he is.
neighbors.shared: a cup of water can cross a line that people drew.

neighbors.heading: what the great ones do
neighbors.text: Today an old monk kept his hard way of life so that people who came later would take heart and try it too. Hindus hear that reason in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a great person does, others follow; the standard they set, the world takes up. So even one who needs nothing still acts, for the good of the world.
neighbors.difference: Kassapa's example is a life of renunciation in the forest. Krishna's point is that Arjuna shouldn't walk away from his duty in the world, but act without clinging, as an example to others.
neighbors.shared: someone you'll never meet may be learning from how you live.

neighbors.heading: planting for those after
neighbors.text: Today Kassapa kept his rag robes in old age, so people in the future would see the path still walked. The Talmud tells of Honi, who met an old man planting a carob tree, a tree slow to bear fruit. Why plant what you won't eat? The man answered that he found carob trees in the world, planted by his fathers, so he plants for his children.
neighbors.difference: Kassapa's gift to the future is a way of life lived as an example. The old man's gift is a tree: in Jewish teaching, caring for the world and for the generations after you is part of serving God.
neighbors.shared: some of the best things we do are for people we'll never meet.

neighbors.heading: the last shall be first
neighbors.text: Today proud princes asked that their barber be ordained before them, so they'd have to bow to him. Christians know that upside-down order. Jesus said: "So the last shall be first, and the first last." And at his last supper he washed his friends' feet, telling them: "ye also ought to wash one another's feet."
neighbors.difference: In the sangha, rank comes from the day you were ordained, so the princes choose the order on purpose. In the Gospel, the one who washes feet is the one his disciples call Lord, showing them what greatness looks like.
neighbors.shared: humility is something you can practice on purpose.

neighbors.heading: the noblest of you
neighbors.text: Today the princes stepped down so a barber could go first. The Qur'an sets birth aside too: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." And the Prophet's first caller to prayer was Bilal, a freed slave, chosen for his voice and his faith.
neighbors.difference: In the sangha, seniority comes from the order of ordination, a rule the princes use against their own pride. In Islam, honor belongs to piety, which only God can fully weigh, so no one can claim it by rank.
neighbors.shared: the person you overlooked may be the one you learn from.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 49:13 (Pickthall 1930) · the Sira, on Bilal ibn Rabah (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: putting away lying
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha taught his young son about lying with a little water left in a vessel. Catholics teach truthfulness from childhood too, in the commandment: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." And Paul wrote: "Wherefore putting away lying, speak ye the truth every man with his neighbour; for we are members one of another."
neighbors.difference: The Buddha shows Rahula what a lie does to the one who tells it: it empties him like a vessel. Paul's reason looks outward: we belong to each other, so a lie wounds the body we share.
neighbors.shared: telling the truth keeps you whole, and keeps others safe.

neighbors.heading: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today a boy learned that a life with lies in it is like a vessel tipped out and empty. Sikhs hold truth very high too. Guru Nanak taught that truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living. A Sikh is asked to earn an honest living, kirat karni, so the truth shows in daily work and not only in words.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha teaches with a picture a child can hold, aimed at a novice monk. Guru Nanak speaks to householders: truth lived out in family, work and sharing, before God, whom Sikhs call the True One.
neighbors.shared: truth is something you do, not just something you say.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62 (Sri Raag, Guru Nanak) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a drop on a stone
neighbors.text: Today Sona began at the very end, old and alone, and became foremost in effort. Jewish tradition tells of Rabbi Akiva, a shepherd who hadn't learned to read by forty. He saw a stone hollowed by dripping water and thought: if soft water can wear down stone, Torah can surely shape my heart. He began with the alphabet alongside his young son, and became a great teacher.
neighbors.difference: Sona's late start is a race toward freedom, practicing day and night. Akiva's is a lifetime of study: in Jewish tradition, learning Torah is itself a way of serving God, with no finish line.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to begin right where you are.

neighbors.heading: learning, late
neighbors.text: Today an old mother of ten began her practice when no one expected anything more of her. The Roman writer Cicero wrote a whole dialogue on old age. In it, the elder Cato says he took up Greek literature as an old man, and argues that the mind keeps its strength if you keep using it, like a lamp kept supplied with oil.
neighbors.difference: Sona's late start points toward freedom from the round of birth and death. Cicero's Cato is after a good life and a calm end within this one, with study and friendship as the oil.
neighbors.shared: the years don't close the door to growing.
neighbors.sources: Cicero, On Old Age (De Senectute) 8 and 11 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the traveler's share
neighbors.text: Today Visakha asked to feed travelers, the sick and those who nurse them, filling each gap she noticed. The Qur'an names people like these. Righteousness, it says, is in the one who gives wealth, out of love for God, to family, orphans, the needy, the traveler and those who ask. Travelers also have a share in zakat, the required giving.
neighbors.difference: Visakha's gifts go to the monastic community, and she finds joy and calm for her own practice in them. In Islam some giving, zakat, is a duty owed to God, and those it reaches have a right to it.
neighbors.shared: real kindness notices who's tired, hungry or far from home.

neighbors.heading: the guest as god
neighbors.text: Today Visakha thought of travelers arriving hungry and the sick who needed medicine. Hindus are taught the same attention to whoever comes to the door. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells a student leaving his teacher: let your mother be a god to you, and your father, your teacher, and your guest. Honoring guests is counted among a householder's daily duties.
neighbors.difference: Visakha gives to monks and nuns, as a laywoman supporting the community. In the Hindu householder's duties the guest can be anyone at all, and serving them is a form of worship.
neighbors.shared: the best kindness notices exactly what someone needs.

neighbors.heading: with the lowest of the low
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha stopped on a city street for a man who carried away dead flowers, and said, come. Sikhs hear the same welcome. Guru Nanak sang that he stands with the lowest of the low, and that God's grace falls where the lowly are cared for. In the langar, the Guru's kitchen, everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same meal.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's welcome brings Sunita into a monastic order, where gods and people come to honor him. The Guru's welcome happens in ordinary life: no one leaves home, and the equal meal is shared by all.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too low for a welcome.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15 (Sri Raag, Guru Nanak) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: follow me
neighbors.text: Today a flower-sweeper asked to become a monk, and the Buddha answered in two words: come, monk. The Gospels tell a call just as short, to a tax collector people despised: "he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him."
neighbors.difference: Sunita was looked down on for his birth and his work, and the Buddha's verse makes worth about how you live. Matthew was scorned for collecting taxes; Jesus says he came to call sinners, not the righteous.
neighbors.shared: a welcome can change a whole life in two words.

neighbors.heading: one swallow doesn't make a spring
neighbors.text: Today a nun was told to fill herself with good things the way the moon fills, night by night. Aristotle saw goodness grow the same way. We become just by doing just things, he wrote, and brave by doing brave ones. Character is built by habit, and one good day doesn't make a good life, just as one swallow doesn't make a spring.
neighbors.difference: Punna's filling ends in wisdom that tears through darkness: freedom itself. Aristotle's goal is flourishing in this life, a person whose good habits have become second nature.
neighbors.shared: goodness grows a little more each evening, if you keep at it.

neighbors.heading: increasing to perfect day
neighbors.text: Today Punna was told to grow full like the moon on the fifteenth night, a little more light each evening. Catholics have a proverb with the same slow brightening: "But the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards and increaseth even to perfect day." The Church speaks of holiness as growth too, step by step, with God's grace.
neighbors.difference: Punna fills herself with good qualities through her own practice. For Catholics, growth in holiness is first a gift of grace, with the person cooperating with God, the source of the light.
neighbors.shared: nobody becomes full of light in one night.

neighbors.heading: good company
neighbors.text: Today Kisa Gotami's song began with friends before grief: stay close to good people, and wisdom grows. Hindus have a word for this, satsang, the company of the good. In Bhaja Govindam, a hymn tradition credits to Adi Shankara, good company brings freedom from clinging, then from delusion, then a steady mind, and at last freedom while still alive.
neighbors.difference: For Kisa Gotami, good friends are the whole of the holy life, walking together on the eightfold path. In many Hindu homes and temples, satsang also means gathering to sing and hear about God.
neighbors.shared: the people around you help shape who you become.

neighbors.heading: two are better than one
neighbors.text: Today a grieving mother sang that good friendship comes first, and that wisdom grows in good company. Jewish wisdom says it too. Ecclesiastes: "Two are better than one... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow." And the sages taught: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend.
neighbors.difference: For Kisa Gotami, good friends lead toward the deathless, freedom from all suffering. In Jewish life, friends also make a minyan, the ten needed for some prayers, including the mourner's Kaddish, so no mourner prays alone.
neighbors.shared: no one should have to carry grief alone.

neighbors.heading: what comes out of the heart
neighbors.text: Today a water-carrier asked a shivering priest: if water washed away wrongdoing, wouldn't the frogs be saints? Jesus was asked about washing too, when his disciples ate without washing their hands. He answered: "There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man."
neighbors.difference: Punnika sends the brahmin back to his deeds: stop doing harm, openly or in secret. Christians keep a washing too, baptism, but understand it as God's grace cleansing the heart, not water doing the work alone.
neighbors.shared: clean hands matter less than what we do with them.

neighbors.heading: he looks at your hearts
neighbors.text: Today Punnika told a priest that river water can't carry off wrongdoing; only changing what you do can. Muslims hold the inner and the outer together. The Prophet taught that God doesn't look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds. And the Qur'an says God loves "those who turn unto Him" and "those who have a care for cleanness."
neighbors.difference: Punnika sets the bathing aside and points to deeds. In Islam ritual washing, wudu, is required before prayer, and a hadith says small sins fall away with the water, alongside a heart turning back to God.
neighbors.shared: what really gets washed is how we treat each other.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:222 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih Muslim, on hearts and deeds, and on wudu (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: joy over one
neighbors.text: Today Angulimala, a bandit who had killed, stopped, and his verse says he lit up the world like the moon freed from a cloud. Catholics honor a man who once hunted Christians: Paul, who called himself "a blasphemer, and a persecutor" yet found mercy. And Jesus said: "there shall be joy in heaven upon one sinner that doth penance."
neighbors.difference: Angulimala's turn still meets the fruit of his deeds: stones and a broken bowl, which he bears. For Catholics, sin is forgiven by God's mercy in confession, while the harm done still calls for making amends.
neighbors.shared: no one is only the worst thing they've done.
