neighbors.heading: Sajjan the robber
neighbors.text: Today a killer stopped, and his name, Harmless, finally came true. Sikhs tell of Guru Nanak and Sajjan, who welcomed travelers to his inn and robbed them at night. The Guru sang him a hymn about bright bronze that leaves a black mark when it's rubbed. Sajjan saw himself in it, fell at the Guru's feet, and turned his inn into a shelter for travelers.
neighbors.difference: Angulimala's change leads him into the monastic order, and he still bears the stones thrown at him. Sajjan's story turns on the Guru's word and grace, and he stays in the world, serving travelers instead of robbing them.
neighbors.shared: a person can stop, turn around, and start shining.
neighbors.sources: the Janamsakhis, on Guru Nanak and Sajjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Rag Suhi, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the middle path
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked a monk who had walked until his feet bled: can a lute play if the strings are too tight? Too slack? Jewish teaching has its own middle way. Maimonides wrote that the right path is the middle one, between two extremes, and warned against piling on hardships the Torah doesn't ask for: what it forbids is enough.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha tunes effort for meditation and freedom. Maimonides tunes everyday traits, like anger, generosity and appetite, and calls this walking in God's ways.
neighbors.shared: too tight or too loose, nothing sings.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 1:4–6 and 3:1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the golden mean
neighbors.text: Today a monk learned from a lute: strings too tight won't play, and strings too slack won't either. Aristotle taught that a virtue of character sits between two mistakes. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between stinginess and waste. And the middle isn't the same for everyone, he said, just as a wrestler and a beginner need different meals.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's middle is about effort on the path to awakening, balanced so the mind can settle. Aristotle's is about character in everyday life, found by practical wisdom.
neighbors.shared: balance isn't doing less; it's doing the right amount.

neighbors.heading: chanted in measure
neighbors.text: Today a monk recited a whole chapter of verses from memory before dawn, and the Buddha praised his clear voice. Muslims carry their scripture in memory and voice too. The Qur'an tells the Prophet: "chant the Qur'an in measure." Someone who learns the whole Qur'an by heart is honored with a title: hafiz, a keeper.
neighbors.difference: Buddhists hold the suttas as the Buddha's teaching, remembered by his disciples and later written down. Muslims hold the Qur'an to be God's own words, kept both by heart and on the page.
neighbors.shared: a voice can carry words safely across generations.

neighbors.heading: what was heard
neighbors.text: Today a monk intoned verses from memory, and the Buddha warned only against singing that pulled attention from the words. Hindus carry the Vedas this way. They're called shruti, what was heard, and students learn them by ear from a teacher, with the pitch of each syllable, using recitation patterns made to catch any slip.
neighbors.difference: Buddhists treat the suttas as the Buddha's words remembered, and wrote them down so they would last. Many Hindus hold the Vedas were heard by ancient seers, not composed by anyone, and the sound itself is sacred.
neighbors.shared: some words are kept best by saying them aloud together.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1, on study and recitation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: answer evil with good
neighbors.text: Today an elephant gave his tusks three times to the man he had saved, and never let the taking change who he was. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a verse of Sheikh Farid: answer evil with goodness, and don't let anger fill your mind. Sikhs also remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who carried water to wounded soldiers on both sides of a battle.
neighbors.difference: The elephant's giving is a perfection built over lifetimes on the way to Buddhahood. For Sikhs, doing good to all comes from seeing God's light in everyone, friend and enemy alike.
neighbors.shared: someone else's ingratitude doesn't get to decide who you are.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition, on Bhai Ghanaiya (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: kind unto the unthankful
neighbors.text: Today an elephant kept giving to a man who kept taking more. Jesus asked his listeners for that kind of goodness: "But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again... for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil."
neighbors.difference: In the tale, the earth swallows the ungrateful man. In Luke, the reason to keep giving is God's own kindness to the unthankful, which Christians are asked to imitate.
neighbors.shared: keep being kind, even when no thanks comes back.

neighbors.heading: the part no one can reach
neighbors.text: Today an ascetic said his patience didn't live anywhere a blade could reach. The Stoics taught something close. Epictetus said people are upset not by things but by their opinions about things. And Marcus Aurelius began his days expecting rude and ungrateful people, reminding himself that none of them could harm the part of him that chooses.
neighbors.difference: Khantivadi's patience is a perfection on the long road to awakening, and he wishes his torturer long life. The Stoics ground calm in reason: what lies outside your choice can't touch your character.
neighbors.shared: there's a quiet place in you no one else can take.

neighbors.heading: they know not what they do
neighbors.text: Today the preacher of patience, wounded again and again, wished long life to the king who hurt him. Catholics hear the words of Jesus on the cross: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." And Stephen, honored as the first martyr, prayed as he was stoned: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge."
neighbors.difference: Khantivadi's patience rests in his own heart, a quality nothing can cut. Jesus and Stephen hand their persecutors to God, asking the Father's mercy for them.
neighbors.shared: hard as it is, mercy can have the last word.

neighbors.heading: the boy at the river
neighbors.text: Today Sama filled a water jar for his blind parents and was struck by a king's arrow. Hindus know a story very like it. In the Ramayana, Dasharatha, a young prince hunting at night, hears a sound at the river and shoots. It's a boy filling a jar for his blind parents. Later tellings name him Shravan Kumar, who carried them on his shoulders.
neighbors.difference: In the Jataka, acts of truth heal Sama, and he teaches the king. In the Ramayana the boy dies, and the boy's father's curse, that Dasharatha too will die grieving for a son, comes true when Rama goes into exile.
neighbors.shared: caring for the ones who cared for you is sacred work.

neighbors.heading: honor thy father and mother
neighbors.text: Today a son was his blind parents' eyes and hands, and his last worry was who would bring them water. Jewish law makes this a commandment: "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land." The Talmud spells out what that means: give them food and drink, clothe them, help them come in and go out.
neighbors.difference: Sama's care belongs to the perfection of loving-kindness, metta, a quality grown over lifetimes. In Judaism, honoring parents is one of the Ten Commandments, written on the same tablets as honoring God.
neighbors.shared: the hands that once held you are worth holding.

items.lessonTitle: The king who saw heaven and hell

neighbors.heading: caught up, and sent back
neighbors.text: Today King Nimi was carried up in a sky-chariot, shown heaven and hell, and chose to go home and keep working. Paul writes of a man "caught up to the third heaven," into paradise, who "heard unspeakable words." Readers often take the man to be Paul himself. He didn't stay there. He went back to his letters and his churches.
neighbors.difference: Nimi's journey is a map of deeds and their fruits, and he goes back to earn his own good. Paul boasts of no reward he earned: what keeps him going, he writes, is grace that is enough in weakness.
neighbors.shared: a glimpse of where the road leads can send you back to work.

neighbors.heading: the night journey
neighbors.text: Today a king was taken up by a heavenly charioteer and shown where deeds lead. Muslims tell of the Prophet's Night Journey: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." In the hadith he rises through the heavens, meets earlier prophets, and returns with the daily prayers.
neighbors.difference: Nimi's tale is a past-life story told to teach resolve. For Muslims the Night Journey happened to the Prophet himself, a sign from God, and the prayer he brought back is kept five times a day.
neighbors.shared: what we glimpse of the end can shape how we spend today.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 17:1 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, the hadith of the Mi'raj (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: handed on by eyewitnesses
neighbors.text: Today five hundred elders recited the teaching together, so it would be held by many mouths. Catholics read how their Gospels began in a similar way. Luke opens by saying others had set down the events "according as they have delivered them unto us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word." The Church still calls this handing on Tradition.
neighbors.difference: The council sets the teaching down by recitation, with no one claiming more than memory. Catholics hold that Scripture is inspired by the Holy Spirit and that the Church's teaching office guards how it is handed on.
neighbors.shared: a treasure lasts when many people carry it together.
neighbors.sources: Luke 1:1–2 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 74–87 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: gathered into one book
neighbors.text: Today the elders gathered the Buddha's words so no one could later decide what they were. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Arjan gathering the hymns of the Gurus before him, along with saints like Kabir and Farid, into one book, the Adi Granth, with Bhai Gurdas writing it out. Later Guru Gobind Singh named the scripture itself the Guru.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's teaching was recited from memory by elders after his death. The Sikh Gurus themselves had the hymns gathered and written down, and Sikhs honor the book as the living Guru, Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.shared: people who love a teaching take care that it isn't lost.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition, on the compiling of the Adi Granth (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: each in its own name
neighbors.text: Today a king carved in stone that honoring another's faith helps your own. The prophet Micah pictures many peoples side by side: "For let all the peoples walk each one in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the LORD our God for ever and ever." And a rabbinic teaching says the righteous of every nation have a share in the world to come.
neighbors.difference: Ashoka's edict asks for restraint in speech and real listening among many communities. Micah keeps Israel's faithfulness to one God, while the rabbis judge others by their righteousness, not their membership.
neighbors.shared: you can love your own path and still honor your neighbor's.

neighbors.heading: a letter on toleration
neighbors.text: Today an emperor told his people to hear one another's teachings and to speak of other faiths with care. Centuries later the philosopher John Locke made a related case. Belief can't be forced, he argued, because faith that isn't freely held isn't really faith, so rulers should let people of different faiths live side by side in peace.
neighbors.difference: Ashoka's edict hopes the essential part of every faith will grow, through respect and listening. Locke's argument is mainly about limits: the state's power ends where conscience begins.
neighbors.shared: listening to another faith can deepen your own.
neighbors.sources: John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: around the ancient House
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims walked slowly around a stupa, always in the same direction. Muslims on pilgrimage walk around the Kaaba in Mecca, keeping it on their left. The Qur'an says: "go around the ancient House." The circling is called tawaf: the body moves around the center, and the heart stays turned to God.
neighbors.difference: A stupa holds relics of the teacher, and walking around it honors him and the path. The Kaaba holds no relic: Muslims circle it as God's House, worshipping God alone, and face it in every prayer.
neighbors.shared: sometimes walking in a circle is how you say, this matters.

neighbors.heading: keeping the holy on your right
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims circled a stupa keeping it on their right, an old Indian gesture of respect. Hindus do the same at a temple. It's called pradakshina: walking clockwise around the shrine, or around a sacred tree or fire, so the holy stays on your right. In one story, Ganesha circles his parents, Shiva and Parvati, as if they were the whole world.
neighbors.difference: At a stupa the center holds the remains of the Buddha, a teacher who has passed beyond. In a Hindu temple the center is the deity, honored as present and alive in the shrine.
neighbors.shared: walking around something precious is a way of honoring it.
neighbors.sources: Hindu temple practice of pradakshina (paraphrase) · the story of Ganesha circling Shiva and Parvati (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you plant, you eat
neighbors.text: Today a thief argued that the mangoes he took weren't the one the farmer planted, and the king still found him guilty. Sikhs sing it plainly in Japji Sahib, the morning prayer: you yourself plant, and you yourself eat. Our deeds are the seeds, and their fruit comes back to us.
neighbors.difference: Nagasena explains kamma as fruit growing from the deed, with no judge outside it. In the same verse Guru Nanak says we come and go by God's will, hukam, and Sikhs trust grace to lift the one who remembers the Name.
neighbors.shared: what we plant today, we'll be eating later.

neighbors.heading: whatsoever a man soweth
neighbors.text: Today Nagasena told a king that the mangoes grew from the one that was planted, so the thief can't escape his deed. Christians have a line from Paul with the same garden in it: "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." Then he adds: "let us not be weary in well doing."
neighbors.difference: For Nagasena, deeds bear fruit on their own, with no one needed to carry it from the seed. For Paul, God sees and isn't fooled, and mercy through Christ reaches deeper than the harvest.
neighbors.shared: small deeds grow, so it's worth planting good ones.

neighbors.heading: the desire to know
neighbors.text: Today a gatekeeper at Nalanda tested newcomers with a hard question, and inside, ideas were argued until they held. Aristotle begins one of his great works: "All men by nature desire to know." He taught in a school where questions were argued out loud, from more than one side, and students carried the habit with them.
neighbors.difference: At Nalanda, learning served the path to awakening, with logic and grammar as tools for reading the teaching. For Aristotle, knowing is its own delight, among the finest things a human mind can do.
neighbors.shared: a good question is a gift you can pass on.

neighbors.heading: faith seeking understanding
neighbors.text: Today we stepped through Nalanda's gate into a monastery that worked like a university. Catholics know that shape. Monks copied and kept books through the centuries, and Benedict's Rule sets hours each day for reading. Anselm, a monk who became an archbishop, described his work as faith seeking understanding: loving God with the mind, and asking hard questions to understand more.
neighbors.difference: Nalanda's learning served awakening, tested by debate among many schools. Catholic study begins from faith in God's revelation, and asks reason to understand it more deeply, not to stand in for it.
neighbors.shared: a library only works when someone opens it and carries it on.
neighbors.sources: Rule of St. Benedict 48 (paraphrase) · Anselm, Proslogion, preface (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the guest as god
neighbors.text: Today monks walked at dawn and people filled their bowls. Hindu homes know this walk too: for centuries, wandering sannyasis, renunciants, have lived on bhiksha, food given at the door. The Taittiriya Upanishad sends a student home with a short list: honor your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest as God, and give with faith.
neighbors.difference: In Hinduism, the guest can be honored as God, and some see the Divine itself receiving the gift. On the alms round, the monk is honored as someone who practices, not as a god, and giving trains the giver's own mind.
neighbors.shared: an open hand at the door is part of the path.

neighbors.heading: giving runs both ways
neighbors.text: Today the person kneeling on the mat was practicing as much as the monk. Jewish teaching says giving runs both ways too. The Torah commands: "thou shalt surely open thy hand unto thy poor and needy brother." And an old midrash goes further: the poor person does more for the householder than the householder does for the poor.
neighbors.difference: Tzedakah, Jewish giving, is a commandment and a matter of justice, owed to anyone in need. On the alms round, gifts go to monks who keep almost nothing, and giving is taught as a freely chosen practice, not a commandment.
neighbors.shared: giving changes the giver, not only the one who receives.

neighbors.heading: the hill, though high
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims climbed Borobudur, carried upward by stories until the walls gave way to sky. Christians have a climbing story too. In John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, a man named Christian walks toward the Celestial City, and at the foot of a steep hill he sings: "This hill, though high, I covet to ascend." Hebrews calls the faithful "strangers and pilgrims on the earth."
neighbors.difference: Bunyan's pilgrim walks toward God and the heavenly city, helped by grace along the road. At Borobudur, one reading sees the climb as the mind moving from desire to formless calm, with no creator waiting at the top.
neighbors.shared: a long walk upward can teach what a book alone can't.
neighbors.sources: John Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), the Hill Difficulty · Hebrews 11:13 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: from every deep ravine
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims left the carved galleries for open sky and one plain stupa. Muslims make a pilgrimage too, the Hajj to Mecca. The Qur'an calls them: "And proclaim unto mankind the Pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." Pilgrims trade their usual clothes for simple white, king and farmer alike.
neighbors.difference: The Hajj is a duty, once in a lifetime for every Muslim who is able, and it is worship of the One God. The Borobudur climb is a walk anyone may take or not, a picture in stone of the mind's path.
neighbors.shared: a pilgrim leaves the crowded world behind and arrives lighter.

neighbors.heading: the patron of translators
neighbors.text: Today Kumarajiva said translating is like chewing rice for someone else: some flavor is lost. Catholics honor a translator too. Saint Jerome, a fourth-century monk, put the Bible into the everyday Latin of his time. His version, the Vulgate, was read in the Church for over a thousand years, and he defended his choices in long letters. He is the patron saint of translators.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the Bible is the inspired word of God, and the Church keeps watch over its translations. Kumarajiva carried the Buddha's teaching with a team of monks, and several Chinese versions of some sutras lived side by side.
neighbors.shared: someone worked hard so you could hear old words in your own tongue.
neighbors.sources: Saint Jerome, the Vulgate and Letter 57 to Pammachius (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: in the people's own letters
neighbors.text: Today a translator gave China sutras people could say aloud. Sikhs care about this too. The Gurus sang in the languages ordinary people spoke, not a scholars' tongue, and Sikh tradition credits the second Guru, Guru Angad, with shaping the Gurmukhi script so anyone could read the hymns. The Guru Granth Sahib is still read aloud in those same letters.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs read and sing the Gurus' own words in the original, and translations are only aids. Kumarajiva's work was itself a translation, and in East Asia his Chinese became the version people chant.
neighbors.shared: holy words are meant for ordinary voices.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition on Guru Angad and the Gurmukhi script (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: turn it and turn it
neighbors.text: Today Xuanzang reached Nalanda and, instead of hurrying home, sat down to read the same hard books again and again. Jewish study knows this well. Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. And the same collection asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the Torah is God's teaching, and studying it is itself a commandment and a kind of prayer. Xuanzang studied the Buddha's teaching and its great commentaries to understand the mind, under a teacher he chose.
neighbors.shared: the best books open slowly, to the one who keeps coming back.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 5:22 (numbering varies by edition) and 4:1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a few masters, read slowly
neighbors.text: Today Xuanzang stayed for years with one teacher and one long text. The Roman philosopher Seneca gave a friend the same advice: "You must linger among a limited number of master-thinkers, and digest their works, if you would derive ideas which shall win firm hold in your mind." Reading everything, he warned, is like a traveler with many acquaintances and no friends.
neighbors.difference: Seneca was a Stoic: he read to steady his own reason, choosing his books himself. Xuanzang studied inside a living lineage, under a teacher, to understand a path the Buddha taught toward freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: depth comes from staying, not from collecting.

neighbors.heading: no reward nor thanks
neighbors.text: Today Bodhidharma told an emperor his good works made no merit, aiming at the scorekeeping in the heart. The Qur'an describes the righteous feeding the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, saying: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." The Prophet praised charity given so quietly the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, a good deed is done for God, and God does reward it, generously. Bodhidharma's "no merit" isn't about a judge at all: it points at letting go of the counting itself.
neighbors.shared: the kindest gift doesn't wait for thanks.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 76:8-9 (Pickthall) · Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the seven given shade (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not the fruit
neighbors.text: Today an emperor asked how much merit his temples had made, and Bodhidharma said none. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches Arjuna to act without clutching at results. In Edwin Arnold's English: "Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them." Do the good thing fully, and leave the ledger alone.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna asks Arjuna to do his duty and offer every action to him, as God. Bodhidharma offers the deed to no one: his "no merit" points past the counting itself.
neighbors.shared: a good deed is finished when it's done, not when it's counted.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 2.47 (Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885)

neighbors.heading: water for every wounded man
neighbors.text: Today we met Guanyin, the one who hears the cries of the world. Sikhs tell of Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water across a battlefield in Guru Gobind Singh's time and gave it to every wounded man, friend or enemy. When others complained, he said he saw only the Guru's face in each one. The Guru, tradition says, gave him ointment for their wounds too.
neighbors.difference: Bhai Kanhaiya was a man serving by the Guru's grace, seeing the One God's light in everyone. Guanyin is a bodhisattva, called on by name for rescue, who takes whatever form will help.
neighbors.shared: compassion turns toward the cry, whoever is crying.

neighbors.heading: Jesus stood still
neighbors.text: Today Guanyin's name meant the one who hears the sounds of the world. The Gospels tell of a blind beggar, Bartimaeus, shouting by the road while the crowd told him to hush: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Mark writes: "And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called." Then he asked him, "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?"
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus is the Son of God, and the one who hears is God himself. Guanyin is a bodhisattva, an awakened being who chose to stay and help, not a creator God.
neighbors.shared: before anything is fixed, someone stops and listens.

neighbors.heading: sauntering
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims walked Kukai's temple road, and the road itself was the practice. Henry David Thoreau, who walked for hours a day in the woods around Concord, wrote an essay called Walking. He loved an old story about the word saunter: wanderers in the Middle Ages who said they were going to the Holy Land, à la Sainte Terre. A true walker, he said, is a saunterer.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau walked alone, to wake up to nature and to himself, with no temple or saint on the route. The Shikoku pilgrim walks a set road of temples, in a living tradition, with Kukai held as a companion at their side.
neighbors.shared: one step at a time, a road can become a practice.

neighbors.heading: two on the road
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims on Shikoku said they walk two together, the walker and Kukai. Catholics tell a road story like that. Two disciples walked to Emmaus in grief after the crucifixion, and Luke writes: "Jesus himself also drawing near, went with them." They didn't know him until he broke bread. Pilgrims still walk the Camino, staff in hand, to the tomb of Saint James.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the companion on the road is the risen Christ, God with us. For Shingon pilgrims, the companion is Kukai, a great teacher honored as resting in deep meditation, not the God who made the world.
neighbors.shared: on a long road, you're less alone than you think.

neighbors.heading: heard and remembered
neighbors.text: Today Tibetan shelves held two collections: the Buddha's word and the teachers' explanations. Hindus sort their sacred books in a similar way. Shruti, what was heard, means the Vedas and Upanishads, held as revealed. Smriti, what is remembered, covers the epics, the law books and the Puranas. And great teachers like Shankara wrote commentaries, honored and studied, on a shelf of their own.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, the Vedas were heard by ancient seers, not composed by any person, and are eternal. The Kangyur is the word of the Buddha, a teacher who lived and spoke as a man.
neighbors.shared: it helps to know whose voice you're hearing.
neighbors.sources: the Hindu division of shruti and smriti (summary)

neighbors.heading: written and oral
neighbors.text: Today the Kangyur and Tengyur stood on separate shelves. Jewish tradition keeps two Torahs: the Written Torah, the five books of Moses, and the Oral Torah, later set down in the Mishnah and Talmud, full of teachers explaining and arguing. Pirkei Avot opens with the chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and on.
neighbors.difference: In rabbinic teaching, the Oral Torah also comes from Sinai, so the explaining is part of revelation itself. The Tengyur is honored but stands below the Buddha's word, the work of later teachers doing their best to explain.
neighbors.shared: old words stay alive when someone keeps explaining them.

neighbors.heading: sell that thou hast
neighbors.text: Today a Vietnamese king set down his crown and climbed a mountain as a monk. Jesus once told a rich young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." Some Christians took him at his word, like Francis of Assisi, a rich merchant's son who gave everything away.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, leaving wealth behind is about following Jesus, with treasure in heaven. Tran Nhan Tong's verses say the Buddha is in your own heart, found by quieting the mind, even while living in the world.
neighbors.shared: less in your hands can leave more room in your heart.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 19:21 (KJV) · the life of Francis of Assisi (summary)

neighbors.heading: the prince of Balkh
neighbors.text: Today a king gave up his throne for a simpler life. Muslims tell of Ibrahim ibn Adham, a prince of Balkh. Sufi storytellers say that while out hunting he heard a voice ask whether he was made for this. He left his palace and lived simply, earning his bread with his own hands, and the Sufis remember him among their early saints.
neighbors.difference: Islam has no monks: the Qur'an speaks of monasticism as something people invented, and Ibrahim stayed within the prayer and law of Islam. Tran Nhan Tong became a monk in a Buddhist order, with robes and a mountain monastery.
neighbors.shared: a crown can be set down, and life gets lighter.
neighbors.sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Memorial of the Saints, on Ibrahim ibn Adham (paraphrase) · Qur'an 57:27 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nothing true and holy
neighbors.text: Today, in Chicago in 1893, Buddhists stood up and spoke for themselves among many faiths. A Catholic was on that stage too: Cardinal James Gibbons opened the Parliament by leading the Lord's Prayer. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council taught that the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, and regards them with sincere respect.
neighbors.difference: The same council teaches that the fullness of religious life is found in Christ, whom the Church must proclaim. The Buddhists in Chicago spoke of the Buddha as a teacher of reason and kindness, with no creator God.
neighbors.shared: hearing a neighbor's faith in their own words is a kind of respect.
neighbors.sources: The World's Parliament of Religions (J. H. Barrows, ed., 1893) · Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: many voices, one book
neighbors.text: Today Buddhists and others spoke side by side in one hall in Chicago. Sikh scripture did something like it centuries earlier. When Guru Arjan compiled the Guru Granth Sahib, he placed beside the Gurus' hymns the songs of saints from other paths: Kabir the weaver, Namdev, Ravidas, and the Muslim Sufi Baba Farid. They are still sung in gurdwaras today.
neighbors.difference: The saints' hymns were chosen because they sang of the one God as the Gurus did, and now they are part of the living Guru. In Chicago, each faith spoke for itself, and no one's words became another's scripture.
neighbors.shared: a wise heart makes room for good words from elsewhere.
neighbors.sources: the Guru Granth Sahib, compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 (summary)

neighbors.heading: words for a king
neighbors.text: Today Nagarjuna wrote plain advice to a king: be generous, don't drink to excess, meet praise and blame evenly. The Book of Proverbs keeps the advice a king's mother gave him: "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine." And: "Open thy mouth for the dumb, in the cause of all such as are left desolate."
neighbors.difference: Proverbs says wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, and a king rules under God's law. Nagarjuna's letter rests on the Buddha's path: ethics, generosity and seeing that nothing lasts, with the Dharma, not a divine lawgiver, above the throne.
neighbors.shared: even a powerful person needs a friend who'll tell them the truth.

neighbors.heading: a mirror for an emperor
neighbors.text: Today a philosopher of emptiness wrote plain advice to a royal friend. The Roman Stoic Seneca did something similar. He wrote On Mercy for the young emperor Nero, saying he meant it as a kind of mirror. A ruler with power over life and death, he argued, should hold it gently, and the best ruler cares for his people like a kind father.
neighbors.difference: Seneca appealed to reason and to the emperor's good name, and history says Nero didn't listen. Nagarjuna's letter points a king toward the Buddha's path, meeting gain and loss, praise and blame evenly, since none of them lasts.
neighbors.shared: good advice is kindest when it's written for one person.

neighbors.heading: water for a thirsty dog
neighbors.text: Today Asanga stopped for a wounded dog, and compassion opened his eyes. The Prophet Muhammad told of a man who found a dog so thirsty it was licking the mud. He climbed down a well, filled his leather sock with water and gave the dog a drink. God thanked him and forgave him. Is there reward even for animals, people asked? Yes, the Prophet said, for every living being.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, the reward and forgiveness come from God, who sees the kindness. In Asanga's legend, the dog was Maitreya all along, and compassion clears the mind so it can see what was always there.
neighbors.shared: the smallest creature in the dust is worth stopping for.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the man and the thirsty dog (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the dog at heaven's gate
neighbors.text: Today a wounded dog turned out to be Maitreya. The Mahabharata has a dog story too. At the end of his life, King Yudhishthira climbs toward heaven with a dog that has followed him all the way. The god Indra offers him a chariot, but not for the dog. Yudhishthira won't abandon a creature that trusted him. Then the dog shows its true form: Dharma himself.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's test is about loyalty and righteousness, and the dog is a god in disguise. Asanga's is about compassion clearing the mind, and Maitreya is the Buddha to come, a teacher rather than a god.
neighbors.shared: how we treat a helpless creature shows who we are.

neighbors.heading: Sajjan turns back
neighbors.text: Today Milarepa, who had caused many deaths, was filled with remorse and went looking for a teacher. Sikhs tell of Sajjan, who looked holy and kept a rest house for travelers, then robbed and killed them. Guru Nanak stayed the night and sang of bronze that shines outside but is black within. Sajjan broke down, confessed, gave back what he could, and his house became a place of worship.
neighbors.difference: In the Sikh story, the Guru's word and God's grace turn Sajjan in a single night. Milarepa's turning begins years of hard labor, because in Buddhist teaching his actions bring their results and he must work through them.
neighbors.shared: a hard heart can still break open and turn.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Sajjan · Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak, Ang 729 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the least of the apostles
neighbors.text: Today the Tibetans kept the worst of Milarepa's story in, right at the start. The New Testament does the same with Paul, who once hunted down Christians. He never hid it: "For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am."
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the turn came through meeting the risen Christ, and forgiveness is God's gift of grace. For Milarepa, no creator forgives him: the results of his deeds remain, and his long practice under his teacher Marpa works through them.
neighbors.shared: the worst chapter of a life doesn't have to be the last.

neighbors.heading: we become what we do
neighbors.text: Today Milarepa showed his student calluses from years of sitting: practice is the secret. Aristotle said the same about character. We don't become good by knowing about goodness, he wrote, but by doing it again and again: "we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts." Habit, repeated, becomes who you are.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle aimed at a good life among other people, with virtue as a well-trained habit of character. Milarepa's sitting aimed at freedom from suffering, working on the mind itself, alone in a cave.
neighbors.shared: there's no shortcut: you become what you do, again and again.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (W. D. Ross 1908)

neighbors.heading: knees like a camel's
neighbors.text: Today Milarepa's last secret was calluses from years of sitting on stone. Catholics remember a saint with the same mark. The early historian Eusebius, quoting an older writer, says of Saint James, leader of the first church in Jerusalem, that "his knees became hard like those of a camel, in consequence of his constantly bending them in his worship of God."
neighbors.difference: James knelt in prayer to God, asking forgiveness for his people. Milarepa sat in meditation, working on his own mind toward awakening, not addressing a God. Both left the body marked by the hours.
neighbors.shared: the real secret is showing up, again and again.

neighbors.heading: action over inaction
neighbors.text: Today old Baizhang wouldn't eat on a day he couldn't work. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to do his work, since action is better than inaction, and even the body can't be kept alive without it. The true yogi, Krishna says, isn't the one who gives up work, but the one who does it without clinging to the fruit.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Arjuna's work is his duty, offered to Krishna as God. For Baizhang, work in the field is simply practice, the same as sitting, done with full attention.
neighbors.shared: honest work, done fully, can be a prayer or a practice.

neighbors.heading: the labour of thy hands
neighbors.text: Today Baizhang said a day without work is a day without food. Jewish tradition honors work too. A psalm sings: "When thou eatest the labour of thy hands, happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee." And Rabban Gamliel taught that Torah study is beautiful alongside a trade. Some great rabbis earned their living with their hands.
neighbors.difference: In Judaism, work stops entirely on Shabbat, a day of rest commanded by God, and the rest is holy too. In Baizhang's monastery, daily work was part of practice itself, and he refused to be excused from it.
neighbors.shared: useful work, done with care, belongs to a good life.

neighbors.heading: whosoever shall call
neighbors.text: Today Honen gave farmers and fishermen one short practice: call Amida's name with trust. Christians know that kind of trust. Paul writes: "For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." And he says it is a gift, not a wage: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the Lord called upon is Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and grace is God's own gift. Amida is a Buddha whose ancient vow welcomes all who call, and Pure Land Buddhists don't see him as the creator.
neighbors.shared: trust can carry you when effort runs out.

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today Honen gave everyone one short practice: a name, said with trust. Muslims keep a practice of remembrance, dhikr: repeating God's names and short praises, often on prayer beads, at work, on the road, before sleep. Anyone can do it, learned or not. The Qur'an says: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Dhikr remembers the One God, Allah, who has no partner. The nembutsu calls on Amida, a Buddha who vowed to bring beings to his Pure Land, and Pure Land Buddhists don't see him as the creator.
neighbors.shared: a few words, said with trust, can steady a whole day.

neighbors.heading: God among the pots
neighbors.text: Today an old cook told Dogen that others are not him. Catholics love a cook too. Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite lay brother in 1600s Paris, worked in the monastery kitchen and said: "The time of business does not with me differ from the time of prayer; and in the noise and clatter of my kitchen... I possess God in as great tranquillity as if I were upon my knees."
neighbors.difference: For Brother Lawrence, the kitchen is holy because God is present there, and he works for the love of God. For Dogen's cook, the work is practice in itself, this hour and these mushrooms, and no one else can do it.
neighbors.shared: the kitchen can be as holy as any hall.
neighbors.sources: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, fourth conversation (public-domain English)

neighbors.heading: the Guru's kitchen
neighbors.text: Today a senior monk cooked for the monastery himself, in the noon heat. Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and serve anyone who comes, all seated together. Sikh scripture even praises a cook: Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, who ran the langar and, the hymn says, gave out rice pudding rich with ghee.
neighbors.difference: Sikh seva is service to God's people, done in the Guru's presence and offered to all without distinction. Dogen's cook practiced in a monastery of monks, and his point was that his own practice couldn't be handed off.
neighbors.shared: feeding others with your own hands is a practice of its own.
neighbors.sources: Ramkali ki Vaar of Satta and Balvand, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: like the rising sun
neighbors.text: Today Hakuin met false blame with three words, Is that so?, and kept caring for the baby. The Talmud praises the same steadiness: those who are insulted and don't insult back, who hear themselves shamed and don't answer, who act from love and stay glad in suffering. Of them, it says, Scripture speaks: "But they that love Him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might."
neighbors.difference: In the Talmud, this quiet strength grows from loving God, who sees the truth. Hakuin's calm comes from treating praise and blame alike, like weather, without needing to be seen as right.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to win an argument to keep doing good.

neighbors.heading: my other faults
neighbors.text: Today Hakuin answered blame and praise with the same three words. The Stoic teacher Epictetus gave his students a line for being spoken ill of: "If any one tells you that such a person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you, but answer: 'He does not know my other faults, else he would not have mentioned only these.'"
neighbors.difference: Epictetus met blame with humor and reason, since another person's opinion is outside our control. Hakuin's story goes beyond words: he takes in the child, cares for it, and never defends himself.
neighbors.shared: you can let a false word pass and keep doing good.

neighbors.heading: I am nigh
neighbors.text: Today a Burmese monk handed meditation to farmers and shopkeepers. In Islam, no priest stands between a person and God. A Muslim, farmer or scholar, prays directly, five times a day, wherever they are. The Qur'an says: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me."
neighbors.difference: Muslim prayer is worship of the One God, a duty for every believer. Ledi Sayadaw's meditation is training in attention and insight, offered to anyone who wants it, with no God addressed.
neighbors.shared: a deep practice can belong to people with busy lives.

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today Ledi Sayadaw said meditation wasn't only for monks. The Bhagavad Gita opens a door like that. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever offers him even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, with devotion, he accepts, and that whatever you do, eat or give can be offered. Later bhakti saints sang this in everyday languages, for farmers and weavers alike.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's way here is devotion to Krishna, offering every act to God. Ledi Sayadaw's way is insight: watching the breath and seeing body and mind change moment to moment, with no deity at its center.
neighbors.shared: the path runs through the fields and the market too.

neighbors.heading: one human race
neighbors.text: Today Ambedkar's vows promised that all people are equal. Sikhs live this at every gurdwara: in the langar, everyone sits on the floor in one row and eats the same food, whatever their caste or wealth. Guru Gobind Singh wrote: recognize all humankind as one. Sikh names make the point too: Singh and Kaur, given to all, in place of names that marked caste.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, equality rests on one God whose light is in every person. In Ambedkar's reading of the Buddha, equality rests on human dignity and the path itself, with no creator God, and taking it up was also a public, social act.
neighbors.shared: everyone sits at the same table.
neighbors.sources: Guru Gobind Singh, Akal Ustat, Dasam Granth (paraphrase) · the langar (summary)

neighbors.heading: neither bond nor free
neighbors.text: Today Ambedkar's vows said all people are equal, and an old Pali picture showed rivers losing their names in the ocean. Paul wrote something close to this for the first Christians: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Old labels stop counting inside the community.
neighbors.difference: For Paul, people are made one in Christ, through faith and baptism. For Ambedkar, equality comes through the Buddha's teaching and is meant to change society too, with no savior who makes people one.
neighbors.shared: the old labels don't decide your worth.

neighbors.heading: short by example
neighbors.text: Today Sariputta followed a monk down the street just because of the way he walked. The Roman Stoic Seneca wrote that people learn more by watching than by listening: "the way is long if one follows precepts, but short and helpful, if one follows patterns." He told a friend to keep a good person always in mind, and live as if that person were watching.
neighbors.difference: Seneca urged learning from an admired person to train your own reason, often a hero from history. In the Vinaya, the example is a living monk on the path, and the teaching he points to leads beyond suffering.
neighbors.shared: how you walk teaches more than what you say.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 6.5 (Gummere 1917) · Letter 11 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let your light shine
neighbors.text: Today a monk taught without a word, just by the way he walked. Jesus said it in the Sermon on the Mount: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven." Catholics remember the saints this way, as people whose lives taught before their words did.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the light comes from God, and good works point people to the Father in heaven. In the Buddha's teaching, a calm way of walking points to the practice itself, and to a teacher who found the way out of suffering.
neighbors.shared: someone is quietly learning from the way you live.

neighbors.heading: the dice game
neighbors.text: Today the Buddhist texts told on their own monks, quarreling at Kosambi. The Mahabharata tells its hardest story in full too. Yudhishthira, the king famed for righteousness, gambles away his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally his wife, Draupadi, who is dragged into the hall. The epic doesn't skip it. It shows the fall, the long exile and the hard road back.
neighbors.difference: The Mahabharata is a great epic of dharma, with Krishna guiding its heroes and gods taking part in the story. The Kosambi quarrel is a plain record of ordinary monks in the Buddha's own community, kept by the tradition it embarrasses.
neighbors.shared: a story that admits failure is easier to trust.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, the dice game (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not a righteous man
neighbors.text: Today the Buddhist texts kept an embarrassing quarrel from the Buddha's own lifetime. The Hebrew Bible does this again and again: the golden calf at Sinai, King David and Bathsheba, a people complaining in the desert. Ecclesiastes says it plainly: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not."
neighbors.difference: In the Hebrew Bible, failure is told inside a covenant with God, who judges, forgives and calls people back. At Kosambi, the monks are brought round by lay followers who stop feeding them, and no divine judge appears.
neighbors.shared: honest stories include the times we got it wrong.

neighbors.heading: by night into Egypt
neighbors.text: Today Tibetan families crossed mountains at night, carrying texts and teachers into exile. The Gospel tells of a family that left home in the dark too. Warned in a dream, Joseph "took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt." Christians remember that the Holy Family were refugees, and Hebrews calls the faithful "strangers and pilgrims on the earth."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the child carried into Egypt is Jesus, the Son of God, kept safe for his work. The Tibetan exile is a whole community carrying a teaching, led by the Dalai Lama, whom many Tibetans revere as the bodhisattva of compassion in human form.
neighbors.shared: people far from home can still carry what matters most.

neighbors.heading: grieve not
neighbors.text: Today we heard about a long exile, and patience that keeps grief from hardening into hate. Muslims remember the Hijra, when the Prophet left Mecca for Medina, hiding in a cave on the way with his companion Abu Bakr. The Qur'an recalls it: "when they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us."
neighbors.difference: The Hijra became a beginning: the Muslim calendar counts its years from it, and the Prophet later returned to Mecca. The Tibetan exile is still unfinished, and its teaching is patience kept without knowing when home will open.
neighbors.shared: leaving home can be a beginning, not only an ending.

neighbors.heading: sister, mother earth
neighbors.text: Today Thai monks wrapped robes around trees to keep them from the saw. Saint Francis of Assisi, in his Canticle of the Creatures, praised God for brother sun and sister moon, and for our sister, mother earth, who feeds and keeps us and brings forth fruit and flowers. The Church names Francis the patron saint of ecology, and teaches care for creation as part of faith.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the earth is God's creation, given into human care, and the praise goes to the Creator. The ordained tree points to the Buddha's teaching of harming nothing, with forests held in the same care as the community of monks.
neighbors.shared: a forest is worth protecting, not only using.
neighbors.sources: Francis of Assisi, Canticle of the Creatures (paraphrase) · John Paul II, Inter Sanctos (1979)

neighbors.heading: air the guru, earth the mother
neighbors.text: Today a strip of saffron cloth made a tree too precious to cut. Sikhs speak of the earth with that same care. The closing verse of Japji Sahib, prayed each morning, says that air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother of all. Some Sikh groups now plant small forests named for Guru Nanak to keep that promise.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, air, water and earth are honored within the one Creator's order. The tree ordination draws on the Buddha's rule against harming plant life and on his life among trees, with no creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: the earth that feeds you deserves your care.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, closing salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a lamp for the ones we lost
neighbors.text: Today a circle of dancers moved together for the ones not in the circle. Jews remember their dead too. On the yearly anniversary of a death, the yahrzeit, a candle burns through the day, and mourners say Kaddish, a prayer that praises God and never mentions death. Proverbs gives the candle its picture: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD."
neighbors.difference: Jews remember the dead by praying to God and giving charity in their memory, without welcoming their spirits home. At Obon, ancestors are thought of as guests for a few days, and the offerings recall a monk freeing his mother.
neighbors.shared: the people we've lost still belong in our circle.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 20:27 (JPS 1917) · the Mourner's Kaddish and yahrzeit (summary)

neighbors.heading: continuing bonds
neighbors.text: Today the living danced in a ring for their ancestors. Grief researchers have noticed something like it outside any temple. In a 1996 book called Continuing Bonds, Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman argued that healthy grief doesn't always mean letting go: many people keep a living bond with the ones they've lost, through memories, rituals and even talking to them.
neighbors.difference: The researchers describe what grieving people do, without saying whether the dead are present. Obon is a religious festival rooted in a sutra, when families welcome their ancestors home and make offerings for them.
neighbors.shared: love for the people we've lost doesn't have to end.
neighbors.sources: Klass, Silverman and Nickman, Continuing Bonds: New Understandings of Grief (1996) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: better than a thousand months
neighbors.text: Today Tibetans marked the day of miracles, when good deeds are said to multiply many times. Muslims know a night like that. In the last ten nights of Ramadan comes Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, when the Qur'an was first revealed. The Qur'an says: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Many Muslims spend those nights in prayer and giving.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the blessing of that night is God's gift and mercy, the night the Qur'an came down. At Chotrul Duchen, the multiplying is the way actions ripen, remembered on the Buddha's day of wonders.
neighbors.shared: some days invite a little more good than usual.

neighbors.heading: the day that never runs out
neighbors.text: Today Tibetans lit butter lamps, trusting that good done on this day multiplies. Many Hindus keep a day like that: Akshaya Tritiya, in spring. Akshaya means never diminishing, and tradition says giving, prayer and new beginnings on that day bear fruit that never runs out. Families give food and water to others and start new things.
neighbors.difference: Akshaya Tritiya is tied in Hindu stories to Vishnu and other deities, and to blessings on a family's life. Chotrul Duchen remembers the Buddha's wonders, though the Buddha himself prized teaching that changes a life over any marvel.
neighbors.shared: a good deed done today keeps on growing.

neighbors.heading: the mind that runs
neighbors.text: Today the mind was a monkey in the trees, grabbing one branch, then the next. Sikhs know that restless mind well. Guru Nanak's Japji, the morning prayer, puts the whole task in a few words: conquer the mind, and you conquer the world. In Gurbani the mind is spoken to again and again, gently, and called back home.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs steady the mind by remembering the one God's Name, and the soul is real and returns to God. The Abhidhamma sees mind as moments arising and passing, with no fixed self behind them and no creator to return to.
neighbors.shared: a restless mind can be steadied, one moment at a time.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 28, Ang 6 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: new every morning
neighbors.text: Today a bad mood was a page in a flip book, and the next page isn't drawn yet. Christians know a fresh page too. In Lamentations, a book written in grief, the poet says of God: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Yesterday's worst page doesn't have to be the last one.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the new start comes from a faithful God whose mercy doesn't change. For the Abhidhamma, the newness is in the mind itself, always arising and passing, with no creator needed for the next moment to come.
neighbors.shared: the next page isn't written yet.

neighbors.heading: the one who craves more
neighbors.text: Today greed was a torrent, carrying things away: a cart at eleven at night, an argument that has to be won. The Stoic philosopher Seneca saw the same current. In a letter to a friend he wrote: "It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor." Enough isn't a number. It's a way of holding.
neighbors.difference: Seneca answers craving with reason and a simple life, so a person stays free. The Abhidhamma goes finer: greed, wrong view and conceit are one family, each a moment of the mind holding on, seen so it can be let go.
neighbors.shared: wanting less can feel like having more.

neighbors.heading: the root of evils
neighbors.text: Today greed reached wider than money: any holding on, even to being right. Catholics name it too. A letter of Saint Paul warns: "For the desire of money is the root of all evils." The Church counts avarice among the capital sins, the roots other wrongs grow from, and pride sits on that list as well.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, greed is a sin that turns the heart from God and neighbor, healed by grace and generosity. For the Abhidhamma, greed is a root of suffering in the mind, seen clearly and let go, with no God to turn back to.
neighbors.shared: a closed hand can learn to open.
neighbors.sources: 1 Timothy 6:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1866 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the discipline of words
neighbors.text: Today right speech was a moment: the mind turning away from a lie it could have told. Hindus guard the tongue too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names words that cause no distress, that are true, kind and helpful, as a discipline of speech, a quiet kind of tapas, right alongside study of the sacred texts.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, disciplined speech is an offering on the way to God, taught by Krishna. In the Abhidhamma, abstaining is a mental factor that arises in a single moment, with no God to offer it to.
neighbors.shared: a word held back can be a gift.

neighbors.heading: keep thy tongue
neighbors.text: Today the right word was a turning away, in the very moment it mattered. A psalm Jews sing says it plainly: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. Depart from evil, and do good." The rabbis built whole teachings on guarding speech, and they warn against gossip even when it's true.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, guarding speech is part of keeping God's commandments, a way of life before God. For the Abhidhamma, it's a factor of mind arising in a moment, with no commandment-giver behind it.
neighbors.shared: what we don't say can protect someone.

neighbors.heading: the company you keep
neighbors.text: Today who you spend the afternoon with became something the mind leans on. Christians have a proverb for it: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed." Friends tip a person one way or the other, and Christian communities gather partly for that reason, to lean on one another well.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, good company helps a person grow toward God, and fellowship is shared in Christ. For the Abhidhamma, a friend is one strong condition among many, alongside food, weather and a quiet room, with no God at the center.
neighbors.shared: who we sit with shapes who we become.

neighbors.heading: the perfume seller
neighbors.text: Today a friend was a strong support, tipping the mind one way or the other. The Prophet Muhammad gave a picture of it. A good companion is like a perfume seller: he may give you some, you may buy some, or you'll at least enjoy the scent. A bad one is like a blacksmith's bellows: it may burn your clothes, or you'll leave with a bad smell.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, good company helps a person remember and obey God. For the Abhidhamma, a friend is a condition among others, food, weather, a place, that leans on the mind, with no Creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: a good friend leaves something good on you.
neighbors.sources: hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 5534 and Sahih Muslim 2628 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: doing good on earth
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva turned the wish for freedom outward, to include everyone. Catholics know a saint who said something close. Near the end of her short life, Thérèse of Lisieux told her sisters she wanted to spend her heaven doing good on earth. The Church teaches that the saints keep praying for the living, still part of one family.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the saints help by praying to God, who alone saves, and heaven is life with him. The bodhisattva vows to work for every being's awakening, life after life, on a path with no creator God at its end.
neighbors.shared: one life can be spent on everyone's good.
neighbors.sources: Thérèse of Lisieux, last conversations, 1897 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 956 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good of all
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva's wish grew wide enough to hold everyone. Sikhs end their Ardas, the prayer said at gurdwaras and at home, with the same wide wish: Nanak, through the Name may spirits rise, and by your will, may all be blessed. Sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not just my family. Everyone.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs ask the one God for the good of all, trusting that it comes by God's will. The bodhisattva makes a vow to work for every being's freedom himself, across many lives, with no creator to ask.
neighbors.shared: the prayer isn't finished until it includes everyone.

neighbors.heading: the soul is pure
neighbors.text: Today a precious statue sat by the road in dirty rags, and people walked right past it. Jews begin the day with a blessing that sees under the rags. The Talmud gives its words: my God, the soul you placed within me is pure. You created it, you breathed it into me, and you keep it within me.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the pure soul is God's gift, and it returns to God. Buddha-nature isn't a soul or self given by a creator; Buddhists read it as a seed of awakening, or as the mind's own nature, already whole.
neighbors.shared: under everything, something good stays clean.
neighbors.sources: Talmud, Berakhot 60b (paraphrase) · the morning blessing Elohai Neshamah

neighbors.heading: the potato in the cellar
neighbors.text: Today the good in every person was gold in filth, covered but never lost. The psychologist Carl Rogers described something like it. He remembered potatoes stored in a dark cellar, sending pale sprouts toward a small far window. People, he said, carry the same pull toward growth, even when hard years have covered it over.
neighbors.difference: Rogers spoke of a natural tendency in living things to grow, a fact of nature, not a path. Buddha-nature points toward awakening itself, and some Buddhists read it as already whole, waiting to be uncovered.
neighbors.shared: something in everyone keeps turning toward the light.
neighbors.sources: Carl Rogers, A Way of Being, 1980 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: with wisdom
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha was a doctor, fitting the medicine to each patient. The Qur'an asks for care in how a message is shared, too: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way." How something is said, and to whom, matters as much as saying it.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the message itself stays one and the same; wisdom shapes only how it's offered. The Lotus goes further: even the teachings can be means fitted to the listener, like the carts promised to the children.
neighbors.shared: the kindest teacher speaks so you can hear.

neighbors.heading: meeting people where they are
neighbors.text: Today a teaching was a tool, shaped to the person in front of it. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna advises the wise not to unsettle people who are still attached to their work, but to keep working alongside them and lead by example. Hindu teachers speak of fitting a teaching to a student's readiness.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the teacher is Krishna, whom many Hindus worship as God himself. In the Lotus, the Buddha is an awakened teacher, not a creator, and even his teachings are means, like a raft put down once the river is crossed.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher starts where the student stands.

neighbors.heading: honest work
neighbors.text: Today a great sutra opened with chores: a bowl, a walk, clean feet. Sikhs see the holy in ordinary work too. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak farming his fields at Kartarpur. And Gurbani says: one who eats what they earn by honest work, and gives some of it away, knows the path.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs earn by their own work while remembering God's Name, and share what they earn. The Buddha lived as a monk on gifts, walking for alms, and the sutra's ordinary morning is about full attention, with no God it's offered to.
neighbors.shared: the everyday is where the path is walked.

neighbors.heading: whatsoever ye do
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha did an ordinary morning completely, then sat down. Christians are told to bring that same wholeness to chores. A letter of Saint Paul says: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Dishes, emails and the walk to work all count.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, ordinary work is done for the Lord, as service offered to God. The sutra's morning offers nothing to anyone; each act is simply done fully, and the teaching is shown before it's spoken.
neighbors.shared: nothing done with your whole heart is small.

neighbors.heading: like a vine
neighbors.text: Today the gift went out and didn't come back on a string. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote something close in his private notebook. Some people do a kindness and keep the account, he said. Better to be like a vine that bears its grapes and asks for nothing more, then bears again next season.
neighbors.difference: Marcus gives because doing good is human nature, the way a vine makes grapes. The sutra lets go further: no fixed giver, no gift, no receiver to hold on to, and so the merit can't be measured.
neighbors.shared: a gift is finished when it leaves your hand.

neighbors.heading: the left hand
neighbors.text: Today the giver was asked not to lean on the gift, or on the picture of themselves giving it. Jesus said something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Give quietly, without keeping score.
neighbors.difference: Jesus adds that the Father who sees in secret will repay: God sees every hidden gift. The sutra asks the giver to hold no idea of self, gift or receiver at all, and there is no God keeping the account.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't wait for a thank-you.

neighbors.heading: speaking of it together
neighbors.text: Today holy ground was wherever the teaching is explained, out loud, between people. Hindus know that kind of ground. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes devotees who keep their minds on him, teaching one another and speaking of him together, and finding joy and contentment in it. Hindus call such gatherings satsang, good company.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the talk is of Krishna, loved as God, and the joy is devotion. The sutra honors the teaching itself, a verse of four lines, and wherever it's explained the ground becomes like a shrine, with no God at the center.
neighbors.shared: a real conversation can make any room holy.

neighbors.heading: two at a table
neighbors.text: Today a kitchen table became a shrine because something good was explained there. The rabbis said it about Torah. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion teaches: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Shekhinah, God's presence, rests among them. No synagogue required. Two people and the words are enough.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, it's God's own presence that rests among those who study. The sutra speaks of the Buddha or a worthy disciple being where the teaching is, and honors the teaching itself, not a creator God.
neighbors.shared: words shared well can make ordinary ground holy.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:2 (paraphrase; 3:3 in some prayer books)

neighbors.heading: no thought for the morrow
neighbors.text: Today the future mind couldn't be grasped: what's here is only planning, happening now. Jesus said something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Today is enough to carry.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells his listeners they need not worry because the Father knows what they need. The sutra's reason is different: no mind, past, present or future, is a fixed thing to hold, and no one is holding it for you.
neighbors.shared: tomorrow's worry doesn't have to live in today.

neighbors.heading: if God wills
neighbors.text: Today tomorrow's mind slipped through the hand: it isn't here yet. The Qur'an has words that let tomorrow stay open: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." Muslims say insha'Allah, if God wills, about plans large and small, from a trip to a coffee.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, tomorrow belongs to God's will, and plans are made trusting him. The sutra simply finds that future mind can't be grasped, with no Creator holding the days.
neighbors.shared: plans are held loosely, and the day is lived.

neighbors.heading: unprofitable servants
neighbors.text: Today the good was made, then not grabbed, like a river nobody owns. Jesus told his disciples something close: "When you shall have done all these things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which we ought to do." The Church teaches that even our merits are God's gifts.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, merit is real before God and comes from his grace, so the glory goes to him. The sutra says merit is gained but not held, because no fixed self is there to keep it, and no God gives it.
neighbors.shared: good done well doesn't need to be counted.
neighbors.sources: Luke 17:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2008–2011 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: in ego they give
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva didn't take hold of merit. Sikhs watch for the same grip. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak sings of a life run by haumai, ego: in ego they give, in ego they take. And Guru Angad adds that ego is a deep illness, yet its cure lies within it too.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, ego is cured by God's grace and the Guru's word, by remembering the Name. The sutra loosens the grip by seeing no fixed self at all, with no God's grace needed.
neighbors.shared: the giving is lighter when the 'I' steps back.

neighbors.heading: like a breath
neighbors.text: Today the world was dew, a bubble, a flash of lightning: real, and passing. A psalm Jews sing says it of a human life: "Man is like unto a breath; his days are as a shadow that passeth away." The Hebrew poets didn't call life fake. They called it brief, and worth noticing because it is.
neighbors.difference: The psalm sets passing human life beside an eternal God who still takes notice of us. The sutra sees everything made as passing, with no eternal maker behind it, and seeing that clearly frees the mind.
neighbors.shared: knowing it passes makes the moment dearer.

neighbors.heading: a river of events
neighbors.text: Today the sutra's last verse pointed at dew on the glass, gone before the keys are found. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote something close in his private notebook: time is like a river of things happening, a strong current. As soon as one thing is seen, it's carried off, and another takes its place.
neighbors.difference: Marcus used this to steady himself and live by reason, accepting nature's course. The sutra uses it to loosen all grasping toward awakening, while warning that passing doesn't mean nothing.
neighbors.shared: everything passes, and this moment is still here.

items.lessonTitle: The jewel in the coat (Kern ch. 8)

neighbors.heading: nearer than you knew
neighbors.text: Today a man wandered poor with a jewel stitched into his coat. The Qur'an speaks of nearness a person forgets too. God says of each human being: "We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." What a person searches far for may be closer than breath.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the One who is near is God, the Creator, always distinct from his creation. In the Lotus, the jewel is the aim of awakening the Buddha placed in his disciples, and no creator is involved.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may already be close.

neighbors.heading: walking over the gold
neighbors.text: Today the treasure was already in the coat. A Hindu Upanishad tells a story close to it. People who don't know the land walk back and forth over hidden gold every day and never find it. In the same way, it says, beings pass through the deepest truth day after day, unaware it's there.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad teaches that the treasure is the Self, the atman, one with Brahman. Buddhists teach that there is no fixed self; the Lotus's jewel is the aim of awakening, a gift waiting to be noticed.
neighbors.shared: the treasure is already where we walk.

neighbors.heading: why call her less?
neighbors.text: Today a young girl awakened faster than the doubters could finish their doubt. Guru Nanak answered a doubt like theirs. In Asa di Var he sings that woman bears us, man is born of woman, and kings are born of her. So why call her less? Sikh women and men can lead the prayer and read from the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak's words honor women as equal before the one God, in this very life. The Lotus story shows the girl's body changing before she awakens, which Buddhists read in more than one way.
neighbors.shared: nobody gets to say who can reach the deepest truth.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, Ang 473 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: neither male nor female
neighbors.text: Today a girl from the sea surprised the wise men who said she couldn't. Saint Paul wrote words some Christians hear the same way: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Churches still differ on what it means for women's roles in ministry.
neighbors.difference: Paul's oneness is in Christ, received through faith and baptism. The naga princess reaches awakening through deep understanding of the teaching, in an instant, with no savior involved.
neighbors.shared: nobody is shut out by the body they were born in.

neighbors.heading: never just a means
neighbors.text: Today a monk bowed to everyone he met, even those throwing stones. The philosopher Immanuel Kant reached a rule from reason alone: treat every person, yourself included, always as an end in their own right, never merely as a tool for something else. Worth isn't earned by being nice. It comes with being a person.
neighbors.difference: Kant grounds each person's worth in their power to reason and choose. Never Disparaging bowed because he saw in each person a future Buddha, someone on the path to awakening.
neighbors.shared: every person you meet is worth a bow.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pray for them
neighbors.text: Today a monk called back his blessing from a distance, out of reach of the sticks. Jesus asked the same of his followers: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." The Church teaches that every person's dignity comes from being made in God's image.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, each person's dignity comes from God, who made them and loves them. The monk honored each person as a future Buddha, someone who will awaken, without pointing to a creator.
neighbors.shared: you can keep blessing, even from a step away.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:44 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1700 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the elephant's cry
neighbors.text: Today Avalokiteshvara heard every cry and came. Hindus tell of a cry heard, too. In the Bhagavata Purana, Gajendra, a king of elephants, is caught by a crocodile in a lake. His strength runs out. He lifts a lotus in his trunk and calls to God, and Vishnu comes and frees him.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Vishnu who answers is the Supreme God. Avalokiteshvara is a bodhisattva, a being of compassion on the path to awakening, honored but not a creator.
neighbors.shared: a cry for help can reach someone who listens.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana, book 8, the story of Gajendra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nigh unto all
neighbors.text: Today a whole list of bad nights, fire, flood, chains, each answered when someone called out. A psalm Jews pray every day says it simply: "The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon Him, to all that call upon Him in truth." No special words required. A true call is enough.
neighbors.difference: Jews call directly on the one God, with no go-between. Avalokiteshvara is a bodhisattva, not God, who comes in many forms to help beings toward freedom.
neighbors.shared: calling out in trouble is never wasted.

items.lessonTitle: I'm sick because the world is sick

neighbors.heading: one member suffers
neighbors.text: Today Vimalakirti said he was sick because the world is sick, the way a parent hurts with a sick child. Saint Paul wrote to a church about the same closeness: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."
neighbors.difference: Paul speaks of the church as the body of Christ, joined through him. Vimalakirti's sickness reaches out to all beings, out of great compassion, as a bodhisattva's choice.
neighbors.shared: love means your pain is never only yours.

neighbors.heading: one body
neighbors.text: Today a sick man said his illness came from compassion. The Prophet Muhammad gave a picture of that closeness. In their love, mercy and kindness to one another, believers are like one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.
