neighbors.difference: The hadith speaks of the believers, bound together by faith in God. Vimalakirti's compassion reaches out to all beings and is part of a bodhisattva's path, without a Creator at its center.
neighbors.shared: when one hurts, those who love them feel it.
neighbors.sources: hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 6011 and Sahih Muslim 2586 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: words that fall short
neighbors.text: Today a finger pointed at the moon, and the finger was needed, but it wasn't the moon. The Church says something close about speaking of God. The Catechism teaches that human words always fall short of the mystery of God, yet they really point to him. Tradition says Thomas Aquinas, near the end, called his writings straw.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, God himself speaks through Scripture and in Christ, so the words carry his revelation. For the Lankavatara, the moon is the truth of awakening, not a God, and words only point the way.
neighbors.shared: words matter, and they point past themselves.

neighbors.heading: beyond thinking
neighbors.text: Today words were a finger, and the moon was further on. Guru Nanak begins the Japji the same way. By thinking, he sings, the One can't be reached, even if a person thinks a hundred thousand times. By silence, inner quiet doesn't come either. The path, he says, is walking in the Hukam, the will.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Guru's word, the Gurbani, is the living Guru, and it leads to the one God. For the Lankavatara, words point to the truth, and there is no creator to reach.
neighbors.shared: the words are a door, not the room.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 1, Ang 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one leads to another
neighbors.text: Today every act left a seed, waiting to ripen. The rabbis saw the same chain. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Azzai teaches: run to do even a small good deed, and flee from wrong, because one good deed leads to another, and one wrong leads to another. The reward of a mitzvah is another mitzvah.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, a mitzvah is a commandment of God, and the chain is a life lived before him. Yogacara's seeds ripen by cause and condition in the mind's storehouse, with no commandment-giver.
neighbors.shared: today's small choice plants tomorrow's habit.

neighbors.heading: never so little scar
neighbors.text: Today seeds sat in a storehouse until a tired evening ripened them. The psychologist William James wrote about habit the same way: "Every smallest stroke of virtue or of vice leaves its never so little scar." We are spinning our own fates, he said. Small acts, repeated, become who we are.
neighbors.difference: James explained habit through the nervous system, inside one lifetime. Yogacara teachers described a storehouse of seeds in the mind, a stream that some held continues from life to life.
neighbors.shared: small acts, repeated, shape a life.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology, ch. 4, "Habit" (William James 1890)

neighbors.heading: counting praise
neighbors.text: Today the breath was counted to ten, and losing count meant simply starting again. Muslims count too. The Prophet Muhammad taught his daughter Fatima to say, at bedtime, glory be to God thirty-three times, praise be to God thirty-three times, and God is greatest thirty-four times. Many count on their fingers or a string of beads.
neighbors.difference: Muslims count words of praise to God, and the counting is itself remembrance of him. Zen counts plain numbers on the breath, with no words of praise, and the count is meant to be put down later.
neighbors.shared: counting can gently bring a wandering mind home.
neighbors.sources: hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 3705 and Sahih Muslim 2727 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bead by bead
neighbors.text: Today a number tied a wandering mind to something simple. Hindus know that rope. In japa, a person repeats a mantra or a name of God, moving one bead at a time along a mala. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among offerings, he is japa, the quiet repeating.
neighbors.difference: In japa, what's repeated is a sacred name or mantra, offered to God. Counting breaths uses plain numbers, no name and no God, and it's a first step, dropped when the mind steadies.
neighbors.shared: when the mind wanders, coming back is the practice.

neighbors.heading: walking in the will
neighbors.text: Today an old poem said the way isn't hard, if we stop grabbing one side and pushing away the other. Sikhs know a way to set that quiet war down. The Japji asks how a person can become true, and answers: by walking in the Hukam, the will, written with you from the start.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Hukam is the will of the one God, and peace comes from accepting it. The poem trusts the mind, just as it is, to meet the way, with no will above it.
neighbors.shared: peace starts where the fight with what is ends.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 1, Ang 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: content in whatsoever state
neighbors.text: Today rain on the day of a picnic was just rain, without the war piled on top. Saint Paul, writing from prison, said something close: "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." He says he learned it, which means it took practice.
neighbors.difference: Paul's contentment rests on Christ, who, he writes, gives him strength. The poem's trust is in the mind itself, already enough to meet the way, without picking and choosing.
neighbors.shared: contentment can be learned, a day at a time.

neighbors.heading: into the woods
neighbors.text: Today a herdsman parted endless grasses, looking for an ox, and found only the evening cicadas. Henry David Thoreau went looking too. In Walden he wrote: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach."
neighbors.difference: Thoreau searched outward, in nature and a simpler life. The oxherding preface says the ox was never really missing; the herdsman only turned away from his own nature.
neighbors.shared: admitting you're searching is the first honest step.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (Thoreau)

neighbors.heading: the restless heart
neighbors.text: Today the search began, worn out, with nothing found yet. Saint Augustine began his Confessions in that same place, speaking to God: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The restlessness itself, he thought, was a sign of where home is.
neighbors.difference: For Augustine, the heart rests in God, who made it and seeks it first. In the oxherding pictures, the ox is often read as one's own true nature, never really lost, with no God to find.
neighbors.shared: a restless heart is already looking for home.

neighbors.heading: for the good of the world
neighbors.text: Today the search ended not on a mountain but in town, among neighbors, with open hands. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna points to King Janaka, who reached perfection through action, not by leaving the world. Act, he says, with the good of the world in view.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, action is offered to Krishna, without craving its fruits, as a duty done for God. The oxherd simply walks among people, with no duty to keep and nothing to offer, and trees bloom around him.
neighbors.shared: wisdom comes back to the kitchen table.

neighbors.heading: don't stand apart
neighbors.text: Today the oxherd came back to the market, buying vegetables and listening to a neighbor. Hillel taught something close in Pirkei Avot: do not separate yourself from the community. Jewish life keeps holiness close to the table and the street, where prayer is often said with others and help is done among neighbors.
neighbors.difference: Hillel speaks of staying with the Jewish community, living by Torah together before God. The oxherd returns after awakening, with no commandments, simply as ordinary company.
neighbors.shared: the deepest path leads back to your neighbors.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:4 (paraphrase; 2:5 in some editions)

neighbors.heading: that nothing be lost
neighbors.text: Today not a grain of rice was left to throw away. In the Gospel of John, after Jesus feeds a crowd with five loaves, he says: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." Many Christians pause before eating to say grace, thanking God for the food.
neighbors.difference: Christians thank God for food as his gift, and the leftovers in the story point to his abundance. Oryoki's care is about noticing how much is enough, and some of the water goes to hungry beings, with no God to thank.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift, so none of it is wasted.

neighbors.heading: be not prodigal
neighbors.text: Today one raised hand said enough. The Qur'an asks for that same measure at the table: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." Muslims begin a meal in God's name, and the Prophet's way includes not wasting food, even a fallen bite.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, eating with measure is gratitude and obedience to God, who provides. In oryoki, the measure is a practice of attention, and the meal's verses honor the work that brought the food, not a Creator.
neighbors.shared: knowing what's enough is its own kind of thanks.

neighbors.heading: o my soul
neighbors.text: Today Ruiyan called himself by name each day and answered yes. A psalm in the Church's prayer does something close: the singer talks to himself. "Why art thou sad, O my soul? and why dost thou trouble me? Hope in God." Not scolding. Just turning back.
neighbors.difference: The psalmist turns his soul toward God, in hope. Ruiyan's call simply wakes up attention, and the koan even asks who it is that answers; there is no God to hope in.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the kindest voice to wake you is your own.

neighbors.heading: o my mind
neighbors.text: Today a monk called to his own mind: wake up, don't be fooled. Gurbani speaks to the mind like that often. Guru Amar Das says: O my mind, you are a form of the divine light; know where you came from. It's a call home, made gently, to oneself.
neighbors.difference: Guru Amar Das calls the mind back to the light of the one God, its source. The koan leaves the caller and the one who answers open, and Wumen warns against taking any mask as the real self.
neighbors.shared: a gentle call to yourself can wake you up.

neighbors.heading: a last song
neighbors.text: Today a Zen teacher left a short verse at the end of life. The Torah tells of a farewell song too. Before he dies, Moses gathers Israel and sings: "Give ear, ye heavens, and I will speak; And let the earth hear the words of my mouth." And the Talmud remembers Rabbi Akiva dying with the Shema on his lips, lingering on its last word: one.
neighbors.difference: Moses' song and Akiva's Shema turn toward the one God, faithful in life and in death. A Zen death poem points at this moment as it is, and calls on no God.
neighbors.shared: last words can carry a whole life.

neighbors.heading: verses in a cell
neighbors.text: Today a Zen teacher left a short verse at the end of life. Plato tells something close about Socrates. Waiting in prison for his death, Socrates, who had never been a poet, spent his last days putting Aesop's fables into verse. A dream had told him, again and again, to make music, and he wanted to obey it before he went.
neighbors.difference: Socrates spent his last hours reasoning that the soul goes on, and hoped for good company after death. A Zen death poem usually makes no argument at all, and some teachers wrote none.
neighbors.shared: facing the end, some people reach for a poem.

neighbors.heading: light upon light
neighbors.text: Today Amitabha's name meant measureless light, shining everywhere with nothing in its way. The Qur'an speaks of light too: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." The verse goes on to a lamp in a niche, glowing like a star: "Light upon light." An-Nur, the Light, is one of the names Muslims give to Allah.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, Allah is the one God and Creator, like nothing else, and light is a sign of Him. Amitabha is a Buddha who was once a monk, honored for his vow, not as the maker of the world.
neighbors.shared: light is a way to speak of what guides us home.

neighbors.heading: lead me to light
neighbors.text: Today Amitabha meant infinite light, and Amitayus meant infinite life. An old Hindu prayer asks for both. It comes from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and Hindus still chant it: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, lead me from darkness to light; mrityor ma amritam gamaya, lead me from death to the deathless.
neighbors.difference: Hindus who chant this may turn to Brahman, the one reality, or to a beloved form of God. Pure Land Buddhists call on Amitabha, a Buddha whose vow opened a land of bliss to all who call.
neighbors.shared: people everywhere ask to be led out of the dark.

neighbors.heading: remember the name
neighbors.text: Today the name was a bow made of sound: Namu Amida Butsu. Sikhs know a practice of the name too. Naam simran means remembering the Name, often by repeating Waheguru, wonderful Lord. Early in the Sukhmani Sahib comes the line: simro simar simar sukh pavo, remember, remember, keep remembering, and find peace.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Name is the presence of the one Creator, remembered until the self melts into God. Pure Land Buddhists call a Buddha's name, trusting his vow for birth in his land.
neighbors.shared: a name said with love can steady a whole day.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262 (Sukhmani Sahib, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: calling on the name
neighbors.text: Today Amitabha's name was called with trust, in Japan and in China. Christians know this too. Paul writes: "For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." Eastern Christians keep a short prayer, said over and over with the breath: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.
neighbors.difference: Christians call on Jesus as Lord and Son of God, trusting that he saves. Pure Land Buddhists call on Amitabha, a Buddha whose vow welcomes beings to his land, and don't speak of him as God.
neighbors.shared: you can lean your whole weight on a name.

neighbors.heading: heaven underfoot
neighbors.text: Today some teachers read the Pure Land as a land in the west and also a mind made pure, right here. Henry David Thoreau, out at his pond, put it this way: "Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads." He went to the woods to live deliberately, to see what ordinary days were really holding.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau found heaven in nature, the frozen pond and the woods, and trusted his own seeing. The Vimalakirti Sutra ties the pure land to a purified mind, trained on the Buddha's path.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may be closer than you think.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "The Pond in Winter" · "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: within you
neighbors.text: Today a pure land far in the west also pointed to a mind made pure, here. Catholics hear something like it in the Gospel. Asked when the kingdom of God would come, Jesus answers: "Neither shall they say: Behold here, or behold there. For lo, the kingdom of God is within you."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the kingdom is God's reign, given by grace, and heaven is also real, the life with God to come. For these Buddhist teachers, the pure mind and the pure land are found on the Buddha's path.
neighbors.shared: heaven can begin in how you see today.

neighbors.heading: teacher to student
neighbors.text: Today the Kagyu teaching passed by mouth, Tilopa to Naropa to Marpa to Milarepa, one ready student at a time. Hindus call such a chain parampara. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says this teaching was handed down from one to another, and the royal sages knew it. The Mundaka Upanishad tells a seeker to go to a teacher, fuel in hand.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the chain begins with Krishna, whom his devotees worship as God himself. The Kagyu chain begins with Vajradhara, a Buddha, and Tilopa, and what it hands on points to the mind's own nature.
neighbors.shared: some things you can only learn face to face.

neighbors.heading: from hand to hand
neighbors.text: Today the Kagyu passed teaching by mouth, one link at a time. Jewish tradition keeps a chain too. Pirkei Avot opens with it: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. Jews call what came down this way the Oral Torah.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish chain begins with God giving the Torah at Sinai, and much of it was later written down in the Mishnah and Talmud. The Kagyu chain begins with Vajradhara, a Buddha, and Tilopa, and still keeps its deepest instructions face to face.
neighbors.shared: every teaching rests on someone who passed it on.

neighbors.heading: add to your faith
neighbors.text: Today the lamrim laid out the path in stages, each step in its order. A New Testament letter climbs a stair of its own: "add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity."
neighbors.difference: The letter's stair starts with faith in Christ and ends in charity, love, as God's gift. The lamrim starts with this precious human life and climbs, with a teacher, toward the awakened heart and wisdom.
neighbors.shared: big things are climbed one step at a time.

neighbors.heading: a little at a time
neighbors.text: Today Atisha wrote a clear path in stages for people confused by everything arriving at once. Muslims say the Qur'an came gradually too, not all at once. Aisha, the Prophet's wife, said the first passages spoke of paradise and the fire; only once hearts had turned did the rules come. Had the first command been to give up wine, she said, people would have refused.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, the order was Allah's, revealing His word to the Prophet as people could bear it. The lamrim's order was set by teachers, Atisha and Tsongkhapa, so a student could climb toward awakening.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher gives you what you can carry today.

neighbors.heading: the day nor the hour
neighbors.text: Today the lamrim said death is certain, its time uncertain, and only practice helps then. Catholics keep the same watch. Jesus tells of ten bridesmaids waiting with lamps, and ends: "Watch ye therefore, because you know not the day nor the hour." On Ash Wednesday, ashes go on the forehead with the words: remember that you are dust.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, watching means being ready to meet God, in hope of Christ's resurrection. The lamrim's reflection on death turns the mind toward practice, for this life and the lives it teaches will follow.
neighbors.shared: remembering death can make today count.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:1–13 (Douay-Rheims) · Ash Wednesday rite, from Genesis 3:19 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: this is your chance
neighbors.text: Today the lamrim said death is certain and its time unknown. The Guru Granth Sahib says it plainly too: whatever is born will pass away, today or tomorrow. And it says what this life is for, in a hymn Sikhs recite in the evening: you have been given this human body; this is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs and Buddhists both speak of rebirth. For Sikhs, this human birth is the chance to meet the one Creator by remembering the Name. The lamrim points toward awakening, with no creator behind it.
neighbors.shared: this life is a door that's open now.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (Rehras, Asa Mahalla 5, paraphrase) · Ang 1429 (Salok Mahalla 9, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: this too is for good
neighbors.text: Today mind training turned every mishap into the path. The Talmud remembers a teacher who met trouble in his own way. Nahum of Gamzu answered every hardship with the same words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good. His student Rabbi Akiva taught a cousin of it: all that the Merciful One does, He does for good.
neighbors.difference: For Nahum and Akiva, the good comes from trusting God, who turns hard things toward good. In mind training, trouble becomes the path because it shows you self-cherishing, with no one arranging events behind it.
neighbors.shared: a hard day can still be part of the way.

neighbors.heading: the obstacle helps
neighbors.text: Today a bad day became the material for practice. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius trained his mind the same way, in a notebook he kept for himself: "that which is a hindrance is made a furtherance to an act; and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road."
neighbors.difference: Marcus was a Stoic: he used obstacles as chances to act with reason and virtue. Mind training uses them to soften the me-first reflex and grow compassion for others.
neighbors.shared: the thing in your way can teach you something.

neighbors.heading: by intention
neighbors.text: Today mind training said: do everything with one intention, and begin and end the day with it. Muslims know this well. The hadith that opens Sahih al-Bukhari says actions are judged by their intentions. Muslims set an intention, niyyah, before each prayer and each fast, and keep words of remembrance for the morning and the evening.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the intention is set for the sake of Allah, seeking His pleasure. In mind training, the one intention is bodhicitta, the wish to wake up for the sake of all beings.
neighbors.shared: why you do a thing shapes what it becomes.

neighbors.heading: do it as an offering
neighbors.text: Today one intention ran through everything, so an email and a meditation became the same work. Krishna says something like it in the Bhagavad Gita: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, whatever discipline you keep, do it as an offering to me. Then, he says, your work stops binding you.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, everything is offered to Krishna, whom his devotees worship as God. In mind training, everything is done for the sake of other beings, with the wish that all of them wake up.
neighbors.shared: ordinary chores can carry a big purpose.

neighbors.heading: the sky's lamp tray
neighbors.text: Today a butter lamp burned before the Buddha, standing for wisdom that clears the dark. Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak once watched an aarti, the waving of a tray of lamps, and sang of a bigger one: the sky is the tray, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls. Sikhs still sing it at night, in Kirtan Sohila.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak turned the lamp outward: all creation is already praising its one Creator, so no tray is needed. In a Tibetan shrine the lamp is lit and offered, light for the wisdom that wakes up.
neighbors.shared: light is how we say: may the dark lift.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 663 (Dhanasari Mahalla 1, paraphrase) · the aarti story (Sikh tradition)

neighbors.heading: a lamp unto my feet
neighbors.text: Today Tibetan teachers said the butter lamp stands for wisdom, the light that clears the dark. A psalm Christians pray says it of God's word: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Christians light candles in church and at home, and at the Easter vigil one flame is passed from candle to candle.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the light is God's own: Jesus calls himself the light of the world, and the candles point to him. The butter lamp is offered, a sign of wisdom that sees things as they are.
neighbors.shared: a lamp doesn't end the night; it lights the next step.

neighbors.heading: make death familiar
neighbors.text: Today Tibetan teachers described dying calmly and in detail, so it wouldn't come as a stranger. The French essayist Montaigne had the same idea. In an essay on why to philosophize is to learn to die, he says to take away death's strangeness: get to know it, keep it often in your thoughts, so it can't catch you off guard.
neighbors.difference: Montaigne looked at death mainly to live this life without fear, leaning on Roman writers, not on any map of what comes after. The bardo teachings describe a passage through death, toward liberation or a next birth.
neighbors.shared: what you've looked at calmly loses some of its fear.
neighbors.sources: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, book 1, "That to philosophize is to learn to die" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the hour of our death
neighbors.text: Today the bardo teachings mapped dying, so a person could meet it prepared. Catholics have long done this too. Old books on the art of dying, the ars moriendi, walked the dying through their fears toward trust. And every Hail Mary ends by asking for help at that very moment: "pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, dying well means trusting God's mercy, with the sacraments and Christ's promise of resurrection. The bardo teachings guide the mind through death toward recognizing its own nature, or toward a good rebirth.
neighbors.shared: nobody has to face the end unprepared or alone.
neighbors.sources: the Hail Mary (traditional) · Ars moriendi (15th century, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: measured for the sacred
neighbors.text: Today thangka painters followed exact measurements, each figure with its own proportions. Hindu image makers know this. Old craft texts, the shilpa shastras, set out how a murti, a sacred image, is to be measured and shaped. When it's finished, a rite called prana pratishtha invites the deity's presence into it, and only then is it worshipped.
neighbors.difference: For Hindus, a consecrated murti holds the living presence of God, who is bathed, fed and greeted there. A thangka supports meditation: a form of awakening to see clearly and, in deity yoga, to become.
neighbors.shared: care in the making is itself a kind of devotion.

neighbors.heading: not one letter
neighbors.text: Today a thangka was painted by exact rules handed from master to student. A Torah scroll is written that way. A scribe, a sofer, copies each letter by hand, with rules for ink, parchment and spacing. The Talmud tells of a teacher warning a scribe: your work is heaven's work; drop one letter or add one, and you could destroy the world.
neighbors.difference: A Torah scroll has no pictures: the scribe copies God's words, and Jewish tradition makes no image of God. A thangka is made of images, figures of awakening painted so the mind can rest on them.
neighbors.shared: some things are worth making exactly right.

neighbors.heading: be still, and know
neighbors.text: Today the mind settled like pond water, and then it could see. A psalm puts calm and seeing in one line: "Be still, and know that I am God." Some Christian monks and nuns pray this way, quieting the mind first, then resting in God's presence.
neighbors.difference: In the psalm, stillness lets you know God, who speaks the line. In Zhiyi's practice, stillness lets you see how things are, empty and arising from conditions, with no God at the center.
neighbors.shared: a quiet mind sees more clearly.

neighbors.heading: rest, then see
neighbors.text: Today calming came first, then seeing. Muslims know both. The Qur'an says: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" And in a well-known hadith, the angel Gabriel asks the Prophet about excellence, ihsan. The answer, in paraphrase: worship Allah as though you see Him, for if you don't see Him, He sees you.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, the calm and the seeing both turn toward Allah, the One. In Zhiyi's practice, the calm water lets you see your own mind and the world as they are.
neighbors.shared: a settled heart notices what a busy one misses.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 13:28 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih Muslim 8, the hadith of Gabriel (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the word honored
neighbors.text: Today Nichiren's scroll made a sacred center out of words instead of pictures. Catholics honor a book of words too. At Mass the Book of the Gospels can be carried in procession, and after the Gospel is read, the priest or deacon kisses it. John's Gospel opens: "In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the Word is a person, Jesus Christ; the book is honored because it proclaims him, not worshipped itself. For Nichiren Buddhists, the Lotus Sutra's title on the scroll holds the heart of the Buddha's teaching.
neighbors.shared: words can be holy enough to bow to.

neighbors.heading: the Word is the Guru
neighbors.text: Today Nichiren wrote a mandala in words, and his followers chant before it. Sikhs bow before a book that is their Guru. Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh named the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as the Guru after him. A hymn in it says: bani guru, guru hai bani, the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, the voice of the one Creator in the Gurus' hymns, cared for like royalty. Nichiren's scroll centers on a sutra's title, with Buddhas named around it.
neighbors.shared: a page of words can become a place you return to.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 982 (Nat Mahalla 4, paraphrase) · Sikh tradition on Guru Gobind Singh (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no greater ancestor
neighbors.text: Today Ambedkar left a system that ranked people by birth, and found equality in the Buddha's teaching. The Mishnah makes the same point with the first human. Why was one person created alone? So no one could say to another: my father is greater than yours. Every person, it adds, is stamped from one seal, yet no two are alike.
neighbors.difference: In the Mishnah, God stamps every person with the seal of the first person, so all are kin. Navayana grounds equality in the Buddha's teaching on suffering and justice, with no creator behind it.
neighbors.shared: no one is born above anyone else.

neighbors.heading: nay, rather they are men
neighbors.text: Today Navayana stood for equality against rank by birth. The Roman philosopher Seneca pushed back against his own world's ranking. Of slaves, he wrote: "'They are slaves,' people declare. Nay, rather they are men." He told his friend to treat those below him as he would wish to be treated by those above.
neighbors.difference: Seneca urged kindness and saw a shared humanity, but he didn't call for an end to slavery. Ambedkar fought to abolish untouchability in law and led his followers away from caste into the Buddha's path.
neighbors.shared: a person's worth isn't set by where they were born.

neighbors.heading: with the sick
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha washed a sick monk and said: whoever would care for me should care for the sick. A hadith qudsi gives the same scene its own turn. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah says: I was sick, and you did not visit Me. How, Lord? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, Allah is not sick; He is near the sick, and visiting them is a way to Him. The Buddha speaks as a teacher, asking his monks to care for each other as they would for him.
neighbors.shared: sitting with someone who's sick is never small.

neighbors.heading: serve beings as God
neighbors.text: Today Buddhist care went into hospices, prisons and disasters. In Hindu tradition, Ramakrishna is remembered for a phrase his student Vivekananda carried into the world: shiva jnane jiva seva, serve living beings as Shiva, as God himself. The mission Vivekananda founded runs hospitals and relief work in that spirit.
neighbors.difference: For Ramakrishna, God lives in the one who is served, so service is worship. Buddhist care serves a suffering being out of compassion; some schools see buddha-nature in them, not a God.
neighbors.shared: caring for someone in trouble is a way of practice.
neighbors.sources: sayings of Ramakrishna, as passed on by Vivekananda (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good of all
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva vowed to free beings without number, not just themselves. Sikhs close their community prayer, the Ardas, with a wish that reaches as wide: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, may spirits rise; by your will, may all be well.
neighbors.difference: The Ardas asks the one Creator, Waheguru, for the good of everyone. A bodhisattva vows to help free all beings, over many lives, through the perfections.
neighbors.shared: nobody's good is complete until everyone's is.

neighbors.heading: the things of others
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva set out to wake up for the sake of all, with long patience. Paul asks for the same turning of the heart: "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." He points to Jesus, who, the letter says, took upon him the form of a servant.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus gives himself once for all, as God's Son, and believers follow him in love. A bodhisattva is a being on the way to Buddhahood, staying through many lives to help.
neighbors.shared: the heart grows when it looks beyond itself.

neighbors.heading: all at once, or slowly
neighbors.text: Today schools stressed sudden awakening or gradual training. The psychologist William James found the same two kinds among the people he studied. In The Varieties of Religious Experience, he described a slow change, built piece by piece, and a sudden one, where a person stops straining, gives up, and finds themselves changed.
neighbors.difference: James studied changes of heart from the outside, as a psychologist, and judged them by their fruits in a life. The Chan schools argue about awakening from inside one path, with its teachers and practice.
neighbors.shared: change can come in a flash, or one brick at a time.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), lectures 9–10 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a light, a castle
neighbors.text: Today awakening came suddenly or step by step. Catholics know both roads. Saul on the way to Damascus: "suddenly a light from heaven shined round about him." And Saint Teresa of Avila pictured the soul as a castle of many rooms, walked through slowly in prayer, toward God at the center.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, both the flash and the slow road are God's grace, drawing a person to him. In Chan, awakening is seeing your own nature, whether it comes all at once or after long training.
neighbors.shared: some find the way in a moment, others over a life.
neighbors.sources: Acts 9:3 (Douay-Rheims) · Teresa of Avila, The Interior Castle (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: whatever way
neighbors.text: Today Dasama said a burning house with eleven doors can be left by any one of them. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says something with the same open hand: in whatever way people come to me, in that way I receive them; on every side, people follow my path.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, every road leads to Krishna, whom his devotees worship as God. Dasama's doors are eleven meditations inside the Buddha's teaching, all leading out of the fire, not to a God.
neighbors.shared: your door can be home without making another one fake.

neighbors.heading: each in its own name
neighbors.text: Today Dasama found his door without calling the other ten fake. The prophet Micah pictures many peoples at peace, each under its own vine and fig tree, each walking its own way: "For let all the peoples walk each one in the name of its god, But we will walk in the name of the LORD our God for ever and ever."
neighbors.difference: Micah's line is about Israel's faithfulness to its God while the nations keep their own ways. Dasama's doors all sit inside the Buddha's teaching, eleven ways out of the same fire.
neighbors.shared: you can walk your own way and wish your neighbor well.

neighbors.heading: let us kneel
neighbors.text: Today bowing ran through every school, from a small bow to the whole body on the floor. Christians bow and kneel too. A psalm invites it: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker." Catholics genuflect, Orthodox Christians make full prostrations in Lent, and others kneel to pray.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the bow is worship of God, the maker. A Buddhist bow honors the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and works on pride, without bowing to a creator.
neighbors.shared: the body can say humbly what words can't.

neighbors.heading: nearest on the ground
neighbors.text: Today bowing went all the way down, forehead to the floor. Muslims do this in each daily prayer: a bow from the waist, then sujud, forehead on the ground. The Qur'an says: "prostrate thyself, and draw near." And a hadith says a servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, prostration belongs to Allah alone; Muslims bow to no person or image. Buddhists bow before images of the Buddha and to teachers, as respect and a remedy for pride, not as worship of a creator.
neighbors.shared: putting your head down can lift your heart.

neighbors.heading: here he was born
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims went to Lumbini, where they can say: here the Buddha was born. Catholic pilgrims go to Bethlehem. Beneath the Church of the Nativity, a silver star in the floor marks the spot. Luke tells it plainly: Mary "brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the child born at Bethlehem is God made man, and the place is holy for that. Buddhists honor Lumbini as where a man was born who became the Buddha, a teacher who woke up.
neighbors.shared: standing where a story began can move you.

neighbors.heading: where Nanak was born
neighbors.text: Today pilgrims went to Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace. Sikh pilgrims go to Nankana Sahib, in what is now Pakistan, where Guru Nanak was born; groups cross the border for his birthday. Yet Nanak himself sang, in the Japji, that he'd bathe at holy places only if it pleased God, and without that, the bath is worth nothing.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the true pilgrimage is remembering the Name; Nankana honors the Guru, not any power in the ground. Buddhist pilgrims go because the Buddha himself named his birthplace as a place to visit and be moved.
neighbors.shared: a birthplace reminds you a great life began small.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2 (Japji, pauri 6, paraphrase) · Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: open thy hand
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said that if people knew what giving does, they wouldn't eat without sharing. The Torah commands it plainly: "Thou shalt surely open thy hand unto thy poor and needy brother, in thy land." Many Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, and some families drop in coins before Shabbat.
neighbors.difference: In Judaism, tzedakah is a matter of righteousness: giving is a commandment from God, owed to the poor. In the Buddha's teaching, giving is the first perfection, freely chosen, loosening the grip of greed.
neighbors.shared: an open hand makes a fuller table.

neighbors.heading: spent on someone else
neighbors.text: Today giving became a daily practice. Psychologists have tested what giving does for the giver. In one study, people handed a small sum of money and asked to spend it on someone else reported feeling happier that evening than people asked to spend it on themselves. The researchers titled their paper: "Spending money on others promotes happiness."
neighbors.difference: The study measured a mood a few hours later. The Itivuttaka speaks of giving as a seed that ripens over a long time, and a way to loosen greed, whether or not it feels good tonight.
neighbors.shared: giving often comes back as gladness.

neighbors.heading: the white days
neighbors.text: Today the uposatha followed the moon, with extra precepts for a day and a night. Islam keeps time by the moon too. Of the new moons, the Qur'an says: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." And the Prophet is remembered fasting the white days, the thirteenth to fifteenth of each lunar month, when the moon is full.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, fasting the white days follows the Prophet's example and is done for Allah. The uposatha is a day of eight precepts, a lay person's taste of monastic life, kept as the Buddha taught.
neighbors.shared: the moon can remind you to begin again.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:189 (Pickthall 1930) · hadith on the white days, Sunan an-Nasa'i (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the eleventh day
neighbors.text: Today the uposatha came with the moon, a day and a night of extra vows. Hindus keep moon days too. Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each lunar fortnight, comes twice a month. Hindus, Vaishnavas especially, may fast or eat simply that day, and spend it in prayer and remembering Vishnu.
neighbors.difference: Ekadashi is kept for Vishnu, out of devotion to God. The uposatha honors no god: it's a day to keep eight precepts and practice more closely, as the Buddha taught.
neighbors.shared: a day set apart can reset a whole month.

neighbors.heading: the wedding day is set
neighbors.text: Today a funeral chant said all conditioned things arise and pass away. At a Sikh funeral, the evening hymn Kirtan Sohila is sung. It pictures death as a wedding: the day is written, friends, come pour oil on the threshold, and bless me, that I may meet my Lord. Sikhs are taught to meet death as God's will, without loud mourning.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, death can be the soul's union with Waheguru, the beloved Lord. The Buddhist chant finds happiness in the stilling of all that arises and passes, and the family makes merit for the one who died.
neighbors.shared: at the end, the people who love you gather and sing.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (Sohila, Gauri Deepaki Mahalla 1, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: dust to dust
neighbors.text: Today a funeral chant named what passes: all conditioned things arise and cease. At the graveside, the old Book of Common Prayer says it as earth falls on the coffin: "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life."
neighbors.difference: The Christian words end in hope of resurrection through Christ. The Pali verse ends in the stilling of everything that arises, which it calls happiness, with no body raised.
neighbors.shared: grief and hope can stand at the same grave.
neighbors.sources: Book of Common Prayer 1662, The Burial of the Dead

neighbors.heading: a friend who told him
neighbors.text: Today monks at the end of the rains asked each other: if you've seen, heard or suspected anything, tell me, out of compassion. Benjamin Franklin did something like it. He kept a list of virtues to practice. A Quaker friend kindly told him he was thought proud, and gave examples, so Franklin added humility to the list.
neighbors.difference: Franklin's project was self-improvement by his own plan, and he admitted humility stayed hard for him. The Pavarana is a community rite, kept every year, where each monk asks the others for correction.
neighbors.shared: the people near you see what you can't.

neighbors.heading: in the spirit of meekness
neighbors.text: Today each monk invited the others to name his faults, out of compassion. Catholic monks keep something close. Saint Benedict's Rule asks a monk who has done wrong to come before the abbot and community and own it. And Paul writes: "if a man be overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, faults are also sins against God, forgiven in confession through Christ. The Pavarana asks only fellow monks, and the amends set the community right, with no God to forgive.
neighbors.shared: correction given gently is a kindness.

neighbors.heading: speak truth, live dharma
neighbors.text: Today's verse said: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. A Hindu teacher sends students home with a short charge like it. In the Taittiriya Upanishad: satyam vada, dharmam chara, speak the truth, practice what is right. And the Bhagavad Gita lists purity of heart among the divine qualities.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, right living also means honoring gods, ancestors and guests, and the Gita's divine qualities lead to freedom. The Dhammapada verse is the teaching of the Buddhas for freeing the mind, and asks nothing of any god.
neighbors.shared: be good, do good, keep your heart clean.

neighbors.heading: depart from evil
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada gave the whole teaching in three steps: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. A psalm Jews pray gives three steps too: "Depart from evil, and do good; Seek peace, and pursue it." Hillel took up that last word: be like Aaron, he taught, loving peace and pursuing peace.
neighbors.difference: The psalm sets this inside the fear of the LORD, the God who hears the righteous. The Dhammapada verse is the teaching of the Buddhas, with purifying your own mind as the third step.
neighbors.shared: turn from harm, do good, and keep at it.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 34:15 (JPS 1917; 34:14 in many Bibles) · Pirkei Avot 1:12 (paraphrase)
